svgUI.hint: Toggle fills and strokes independently to inspect meshes generated from SVG paths.

svgLesson.conceptLead: Convert SVG paths into flat meshes in the scene.
svgLesson.conceptBody: Svg uses Three.js SVGLoader to parse vector content and converts supported fills and strokes into meshes. The result can be positioned and scaled as scene objects; it is not browser SVG DOM.

conceptCards.title: Paths and styles
conceptCards.body: An SVG describes outlines and their fills and strokes; this example uses several simple shapes.

conceptCards.title: Can fill and stroke be controlled separately?
conceptCards.body: Yes. Fill and stroke generate separate geometry; skipFill and skipStrokes independently control whether each is omitted.

conceptCards.title: Scene coordinates
conceptCards.body: SVG coordinates must be mapped to scene units. The component flips Y internally; the example also uses position and scale to center the artwork.

svgLesson.purposeLead: Why not use the SVG as a texture on a plane?
svgLesson.purposeBody: A texture is useful for displaying a complete image on a plane. Svg converts supported outlines into scene meshes, allowing fill or stroke generation to be skipped separately and mesh properties to be configured.

purposeCards.title: Reuse simple vector art
purposeCards.body: Place an existing icon or mark as a scene object without first modeling an equivalent mesh by hand.

purposeCards.title: Control parts separately
purposeCards.body: skipFill and skipStrokes control the two geometry types; material and mesh properties can also be overridden when needed.

svgLesson.demoLead: Separate fill and stroke to see how the SVG is built.
svgLesson.demoBody: The source spans 200 × 120 SVG units. Use the switches to select generated parts, then scale the artwork in the scene.

experiments.title: 01 · Stroke only
experiments.body: Reset and turn fill off: colored areas disappear and only defined strokes remain, showing that stroke geometry is generated separately.

experiments.title: 02 · Fill only
experiments.body: Turn fill back on, then turn stroke off: the outlines disappear while the interior shapes remain.

experiments.title: 03 · Scale and position
experiments.body: Reset and adjust scale. The artwork grows or shrinks in the scene; this demo also adjusts its position to keep it centered.

svgLesson.parameterLead: Provide the source, then choose geometry and styling.
svgLesson.parameterNote: src accepts a URL or an inline string beginning with <svg; the other options control fills, strokes and scene transforms. The table describes installed drei 10.7.9.
parameters: Provide an SVG URL or inline string beginning with <svg.
Override properties of the corresponding meshBasicMaterial.
Props passed to fill or stroke meshes.
Here scale=0.015 maps the 200 × 120 source coordinate bounds to 3 × 1.8 scene units; position also changes to center it.
svgLesson.codeLead: Start with the minimal example, then connect the key code to the experiment.

codeNotes.title: 01 · Read the source
codeNotes.body: src points to a local SVG and Suspense waits for it. Its paths and styles determine which shapes can be generated.

codeNotes.title: 02 · Select geometry
codeNotes.body: skipFill and skipStrokes independently skip fill and stroke geometry; the panel visibility switches invert those skip props.

codeNotes.title: 03 · Convert coordinates
codeNotes.body: The source spans 200 × 120. The demo uses position [−100 × scale, 60 × scale, 0] with the internal Y flip to center the scaled artwork.

svgLesson.applicationsLead: Use simple vector artwork as a scene object.

applications.title: Signs in a scene
applications.body: Place a simple direction sign or badge in a virtual exhibition and transform it with the scene.

applications.title: Flat diagram display
applications.body: Convert suitable existing icons or diagrams to meshes and control fill and stroke visibility separately.

svgLesson.boundariesLead: Check SVG feature support and generated geometry size first.

boundaries.title: Complex browser SVG
boundaries.body: SVGLoader does not implement every browser SVG feature; validate filters and complex styling for each asset.

boundaries.title: Many paths
boundaries.body: Complex paths and strokes can create more geometry and meshes, affecting load and rendering costs; compare a texture approach for large collections.

boundaries.title: Physical thickness
boundaries.body: The result is planar geometry and SVG units are not inherently meters. Model or extrude thickness separately and define the unit conversion.

conceptDetails: SVG describes graphics with paths, fills and strokes. For a bordered circle, the interior color is the fill and the outline is the stroke; Svg parses those descriptions and turns supported parts into Three.js meshes.

Unlike using the entire SVG as a texture, this component can skip fill and stroke independently. The result is still planar scene geometry: it has no automatic thickness and is not browser SVG DOM styled with CSS.
The example source spans 200 × 120 coordinates. At scale=0.015 that range is about 3 × 1.8 scene units; the component flips Y internally and the demo translates the artwork toward the origin.
purposeDetails: Creating scene geometry manually requires loading and parsing SVG paths, converting fills to shapes, generating stroke geometry and setting materials and coordinate orientation. Svg packages these steps and allows fill and stroke to be configured separately.

A texture may be better for simply displaying a complex illustration; Svg can be useful when handling simple outlines separately. SVGLoader does not support all browser SVG features, so validate the actual asset.
codeDetails: src points to a local SVG and Suspense waits for loading. Svg parses the paths and generates fill and stroke meshes; skipFill and skipStrokes independently omit each kind.

The panel expresses “show fill” and “show stroke,” so the live code inverts those values for the skip props. Position [−100 × scale, 60 × scale, 0] works with the internal Y flip to center the 200 × 120 source bounds.

imageUI.imageHint: Compare LEFT and RIGHT markers to see cropping at different frame ratios.
imageUI.aspectHint: useAspect calculates viewport-covering dimensions from the image ratio; a factor below 1 scales the result down.

imageLesson.conceptLead: Place an image in a 3D scene.
imageLesson.conceptBody: Image creates a textured plane that can be positioned and scaled like other scene objects. It also provides cover-like cropping, zoom, grayscale and rounded corners.

conceptCards.title: Source ratio
conceptCards.body: The source is 960 × 540, with a 16:9 aspect ratio; this describes the image itself.

conceptCards.title: Resize the frame or zoom the image?
conceptCards.body: scale changes the scene plane’s width and height; zoom enlarges the image inside the unchanged frame. Use scale for a larger board and zoom to emphasize central detail.

conceptCards.title: Cover cropping
conceptCards.body: When the image and frame ratios differ, the image preserves its proportions and fills the frame; excess content is cropped.

imageLesson.purposeLead: Why not put a texture on a plane directly?
imageLesson.purposeBody: A basic textured plane can display an image, but matching different frame and image ratios requires texture-coordinate work. Grayscale and rounded corners also need material handling. Image exposes these common effects as parameters.

purposeCards.title: Less repeated work
purposeCards.body: Load an image and adjust cropping and styling with props instead of writing a shader for each image.

purposeCards.title: Part of the scene
purposeCards.body: The image is still a scene plane: it can follow a parent transform and responds to the camera viewpoint.

imageLesson.demoLead: Change the frame shape and watch what gets cropped.
imageLesson.demoBody: The image has markers at its left and right edges to make cropping visible. The default frame is 3 × 2 m, a ratio of 1.5; the source ratio is about 1.78, so even the initial frame crops a little at the sides. Reset before each experiment and observe both the picture and panel values.

experiments.title: 01 · Compare cropping
experiments.body: Reset, then reduce width from 3 m to 1 m while keeping height at 2 m. The frame ratio changes from 1.5 to 0.5, much narrower than the source; the image keeps its ratio, so the side markers leave the visible area.

experiments.title: 02 · Zoom the image
experiments.body: Reset, then increase zoom from 1 to 2. The central graphic grows and less edge content remains, while the frame stays 3 × 2 m. Moving the camera also changes the frame’s apparent screen size; zoom changes sampling inside it.

experiments.title: 03 · Change styling
experiments.body: Reset, set grayscale to 1, then increase the radius. The first mixes image colors and the second makes the corners transparent; these change material output, not the image file.

imageLesson.parameterLead: Start with the source, frame and cropping, then adjust styling.
imageLesson.parameterNote: url or texture supplies the image; scale sizes the plane; zoom changes the sampled area. The table describes the installed drei 10.7.9.
parameters: Supply a URL or Three.js Texture; at least one is required.
Sets plane width and height in scene units; use it to enlarge the display board. Changing the ratio also changes cropping.
1 uses the original sampling range; increasing it enlarges the content and shows less of it without resizing the frame.
0 preserves color and 1 is fully grayscale; intermediate values blend the two without changing the asset.
Rounded-corner radius on the image plane; this demo enables transparency.
imageLesson.codeLead: Follow the path from source image to texture and plane.

codeNotes.title: 01 · Load the source
codeNotes.body: url points to the local SVG image; Suspense waits while the texture loads. Use the correct asset URL when deploying under a subpath.

codeNotes.title: 02 · Size the frame
codeNotes.body: The first two scale values set the plane width and height in the scene; they do not modify the source image.

codeNotes.title: 03 · Change the appearance
codeNotes.body: zoom, grayscale and radius correspond to the panel controls; transparent allows the area outside the rounded corners to be transparent.

imageLesson.applicationsLead: Use for images positioned as objects in a scene.

applications.title: Posters in a virtual exhibition
applications.body: For posters of different dimensions in uniform frames, set a common scale and let Image fill each frame while preserving source proportions.

applications.title: A rotating product display
applications.body: Place an image beside a model as a display board that moves and rotates with the scene; adjust grayscale when a desaturated treatment is needed.

imageLesson.boundariesLead: First decide whether cropping is acceptable.

boundaries.title: Charts or documents that must remain complete
boundaries.body: Cover cropping can hide text or data at the edges. To keep all content, match the frame to the source ratio, such as 3.2 × 1.8 m for this image; if the frame must stay fixed, use a contain-style approach that permits empty space.

boundaries.title: Cross-origin requests and failures
boundaries.body: Remote images must be accessible and satisfy cross-origin rules; production interfaces should also handle loading and failure.

boundaries.title: Many high-resolution images
boundaries.body: Images consume texture memory. Limit asset count and resolution according to device capabilities.

conceptDetails: Imagine a landscape poster: the source is 960 × 540, with an aspect ratio of about 1.78. Stretching it into a square frame would distort its contents. Image instead preserves the source ratio and fills the frame; to avoid empty space, content beyond the left and right edges is cropped.

If the frame is wider than the source, the image instead fills its width and excess content is cropped from the top and bottom. Cropping changes the sampled region on the plane, not the source file. Matching image and frame ratios requires no edge cropping to fill the frame.

Separate three sizes: source pixel dimensions determine the image ratio; scale determines the plane’s scene dimensions; the camera and distance determine its apparent size on screen. zoom enlarges the content inside the frame without changing the plane dimensions.
purposeDetails: A manual implementation typically loads a texture, creates a plane and material, then calculates texture coordinates from the image and plane ratios. Grayscale and rounded corners need additional material logic. Image combines these steps behind adjustable props.

It is not the only way to show an image: a textured plane suits custom materials or texture coordinates; Html is an option for web buttons, selectable text or forms. Choose according to whether you need an image surface in the scene or a web interface.
codeDetails: The minimal example creates a Canvas and uses Suspense while the image texture loads. Image points to public/images/crop-demo.svg; supply that asset when copying the example and adjust its URL when deploying under a subpath.

scale={[3, 2]} makes the plane 3 m wide and 2 m high in this scene. Image calculates cover cropping from the source and plane ratios. The live code reflects panel state: width and height change the plane, while zoom, grayscale and radius change how the image is displayed.

useAspectLesson.conceptLead: Calculate dimensions that cover the viewport while preserving the source ratio.
useAspectLesson.conceptBody: useAspect takes source width, height and a factor and returns a scale for a scene object. At factor 1 the result preserves the source ratio and covers the current R3F viewport; a mismatched ratio extends beyond the viewport on one axis.

conceptCards.title: Source dimensions
conceptCards.body: 960 and 540 establish a 16:9 ratio; they are not directly used as scene meters.

conceptCards.title: Current viewport
conceptCards.body: The R3F viewport describes the scene area visible to the camera at its target, in scene units.

conceptCards.title: Does the return value display the image?
conceptCards.body: No. It returns a [width, height, 1] scale array and does not load an asset; this demo passes its first two values to Image, which displays the picture.

useAspectLesson.purposeLead: Why calculate dimensions from the viewport?
useAspectLesson.purposeBody: When the canvas size or camera changes, a fixed plane can leave gaps or crop more than intended. useAspect derives cover dimensions from the source ratio and current viewport without manually comparing their aspect ratios.

purposeCards.title: Preserve proportions
purposeCards.body: The dimensions follow the source ratio instead of stretching width and height independently to fill the viewport.

purposeCards.title: Respond to viewport changes
purposeCards.body: The hook updates with the R3F viewport; whether it covers a particular plane also depends on that plane’s depth.

useAspectLesson.demoLead: Compare the factor with the resulting coverage.
useAspectLesson.demoBody: The panel displays the calculated scene width and height. The source is fixed at 960 × 540 and the image plane is at the scene origin.

experiments.title: 01 · Cover the viewport
experiments.body: Set factor to 1: the image covers at least the viewport width and height. If the ratios differ, one direction extends beyond the screen.

experiments.title: 02 · Scale the result
experiments.body: Reduce factor from 1 to 0.8. Both displayed dimensions become 80% of their previous values, so full coverage is no longer guaranteed.

experiments.title: 03 · Resize the canvas
experiments.body: Change the browser window width and observe the dimensions and cropping. The hook recalculates for the viewport while preserving the source ratio.

useAspectLesson.parameterLead: Supply the source ratio, then choose a scale factor.
useAspectLesson.parameterNote: Width and height must use the same units and be positive; factor defaults to 1. This demo starts at 0.8, so it does not guarantee full coverage.
parameters: Define the ratio, not target meters; 960/540 and 16/9 produce the same proportional result.
Multiplies the calculated width and height; 1 covers the current viewport, while values below 1 can reveal gaps.
Three-axis scale computed from the current R3F viewport; z is 1.
useAspectLesson.codeLead: Start with the minimal example, then connect the key code to the experiment.

codeNotes.title: 01 · Read the viewport
codeNotes.body: Call useAspect inside Canvas so it can read the current R3F viewport.

codeNotes.title: 02 · Supply the ratio
codeNotes.body: 960 and 540 describe the source dimensions; the third argument scales the result. These arguments do not load the image.

codeNotes.title: 03 · Apply the result
codeNotes.body: Pass the first two returned values to Image scale; its url still loads the texture separately.

useAspectLesson.applicationsLead: Use for scene planes sized to the camera viewport.

applications.title: A scene background
applications.body: With a fixed camera and a background plane at the viewport’s target depth, factor 1 preserves the source ratio while covering the view.

applications.title: A responsive display plane
applications.body: As the canvas changes size, update the plane from the current viewport instead of maintaining separate formulas for each screen ratio.

useAspectLesson.boundariesLead: The result depends on the current viewport and may extend beyond the screen.

boundaries.title: The entire image must be visible
boundaries.body: Covering the viewport can put some of the image outside the screen; use contain-style sizing when the full image must remain visible.

boundaries.title: A plane at another depth
boundaries.body: A perspective camera sees a different area at each depth. This hook uses the current R3F viewport; calculate the viewport at the target depth when the plane is elsewhere.

boundaries.title: A reduced factor
boundaries.body: A factor below 1 shrinks the cover dimensions and can leave gaps; it does not guarantee full viewport coverage.

conceptDetails: Imagine using a 16:9 image as a scene background while the canvas changes with the window. A fixed-size plane can leave gaps at some aspect ratios; stretching width and height independently fills the view but distorts the image.

useAspect takes source dimensions and a factor, reads the current R3F viewport and calculates plane dimensions that preserve the source ratio. At factor 1 those dimensions cover the current viewport; when ratios differ, one axis extends beyond the screen.

For an 8 m × 6 m viewport and a 16:9 source, preserving the ratio at 6 m height gives about 10.67 m width. That extends past the sides; multiplying by 0.8 gives about 8.53 × 4.8 m, which no longer guarantees coverage.
purposeDetails: A manual calculation compares source and viewport ratios, chooses the axis that fills the view and derives the other dimension, then repeats when the viewport changes. useAspect provides that calculation; it does not load an image or create a plane.

Image displays and crops the picture; useAspect calculates viewport-based dimensions. They can be combined or used separately. If the full image must remain visible with gaps allowed, use a contain-style calculation instead.
codeDetails: Call useAspect(960, 540, factor) inside Canvas because the hook reads the R3F viewport. The common units of 960 and 540 determine a ratio; the result is [width, height, 1] in scene units.

The example passes the first two values to Image scale and loads the source separately with url. The panel shows those dimensions; changing factor from 1 to 0.8 multiplies both by 0.8 without regenerating the image.

textUI.textHint: Text uses local Roboto; adjust width and alignment to observe wrapping.
textUI.text3dHint: Text3D uses local Helvetiker data; bevel expands edge dimensions.

textLesson.conceptLead: Render flat text as part of a 3D scene.
textLesson.conceptBody: Text uses Troika signed-distance-field (SDF) glyphs: stored distance information lets it calculate glyph edges at different display sizes. It supports wrapping, alignment and letter spacing but has no extruded sides; font loading and glyph generation are asynchronous.

conceptCards.title: Font and glyphs
conceptCards.body: font points to a font file. The file must contain the characters to be displayed.

conceptCards.title: Layout width
conceptCards.body: maxWidth constrains text layout and can trigger wrapping; textAlign controls how lines align.

conceptCards.title: Text anchor
conceptCards.body: anchorX and anchorY align the whole text block to its scene position; textAlign instead aligns lines inside that block.

textLesson.purposeLead: Why use Text instead of making a text texture by hand?
textLesson.purposeBody: Drawing text into an image and mapping it to a plane often means regenerating the texture when content changes and implementing layout yourself. Text takes a string and font and provides scene text layout suitable for changing labels.

purposeCards.title: Change content directly
purposeCards.body: Pass a string as a React child and control font size and layout with props.

purposeCards.title: Lay out text in the scene
purposeCards.body: Text participates in scene position and rotation. Compared with extruded Text3D, it suits flat labels and paragraphs.

textLesson.demoLead: Compare font size, width and alignment using the same text.
textLesson.demoBody: This example uses local Roboto and includes a manual line break. Automatic wrapping also depends on font size, spacing and maximum width.

experiments.title: 01 · Wrap lines
experiments.body: Reset, then reduce maximum width. Existing lines break into more lines: the layout is constrained rather than the font shrinking.

experiments.title: 02 · Change size
experiments.body: Reset and increase font size. Glyphs grow in the scene and fewer characters fit on a line, which may cause additional wrapping.

experiments.title: 03 · Align and space
experiments.body: Change letter spacing and switch between left, center and right. Compare line positions; the whole block remains centered on this demo’s anchor.

textLesson.parameterLead: Choose a font and size, then set wrapping, alignment and anchors.
textLesson.parameterNote: fontSize and maxWidth use scene units; letterSpacing is relative to font size. The table describes the installed drei 10.7.9.
parameters: Font URL; ensure the font contains the needed glyphs.
Uses scene units rather than CSS pixels; increasing size can create more wrapping at the same line width.
Constrains layout without shrinking the font; this demo wraps at spaces, so a long individual word may still exceed the width.
Additional letter spacing relative to font size.
Aligns lines within the block; use anchors or position to place the whole block.
Text geometry alignment relative to its anchor.
Preloads expected glyphs; it does not add missing glyphs to the font.
textLesson.codeLead: Start with the minimal example, then connect the key code to the experiment.

codeNotes.title: 01 · Load the font
codeNotes.body: font points to a local TTF; Suspense provides a waiting boundary for font preloading. Check glyph coverage when changing languages.

codeNotes.title: 02 · Set the layout
codeNotes.body: fontSize controls size and maxWidth constrains lines; letterSpacing and textAlign control spacing and line alignment.

codeNotes.title: 03 · Position the block
codeNotes.body: anchorX="center" and anchorY="middle" align the block center to its scene anchor; textAlign controls the lines within it.

textLesson.applicationsLead: Use for flat text that needs to move with the scene.

applications.title: Exhibition labels
applications.body: Attach a title and short description to a model, updating the string and layout as needed.

applications.title: 3D data annotations
applications.body: Place values and names beside a chart or device so they follow scene coordinates.

textLesson.boundariesLead: Decide whether you need physical depth or web semantics.

boundaries.title: Physical sides
boundaries.body: Text does not generate extruded sides. Consider Text3D when the letters need thickness, bevels and volumetric lighting.

boundaries.title: Font coverage and loading
boundaries.body: The example font primarily covers Latin text; other scripts need a font with the required glyphs and a loading state.

boundaries.title: Accessibility and cost
boundaries.body: Canvas text is not native DOM text; provide accessible web content for important information. Measure layout and rendering cost for many frequently changing labels.

conceptDetails: Imagine attaching a changing description to equipment in a scene. Text takes a string and draws flat scene text; it can move or rotate with the equipment, but has no physical sides.

The font determines available glyphs and their outlines; fontSize controls scene size and maxWidth controls available line width. In this demo a narrower width moves words to additional lines at available break points without automatically reducing font size.

textAlign aligns individual lines within the block; anchorX and anchorY position the entire block relative to its 3D anchor. Aligning lines and positioning the whole block beside an object are different tasks.
purposeDetails: With a text image mapped as a texture, changing content commonly means redrawing the image; wrapping, spacing and alignment also need maintenance. Text connects font and layout to R3F so those choices can be described as props.

SDF uses distance information to calculate glyph edges and can keep text crisp at different displayed sizes, but it is not extruded geometry. Choose Text3D for physical sides, or consider Html for selection, forms or web semantics.
codeDetails: The example font points to a local TTF and Suspense waits for font preloading; the font must contain the actual characters. The string is a Text child, while fontSize and maxWidth set its size and layout width.

The live experiment also adjusts letterSpacing and textAlign and uses anchorX="center" and anchorY="middle" to align the block center to its scene anchor. Compare the number and positions of lines as layout changes.

text3DLesson.conceptLead: Turn font outlines into letters with 3D depth.
text3DLesson.conceptBody: Text3D generates glyph geometry from Three.js typeface JSON and extrudes it along a depth axis. The result is a mesh that can use materials and receive light, with different tradeoffs from flat SDF Text.

conceptCards.title: Font outlines
conceptCards.body: font supplies glyph outlines in typeface JSON; a regular TTF or WOFF file cannot be passed directly.

conceptCards.title: Size or thickness?
conceptCards.body: size changes the overall glyph size; height controls extrusion along the depth axis. Adjust height to make only the sides deeper.

conceptCards.title: Bevel
conceptCards.body: Enabling bevel creates a sloped edge; material and lighting help make that edge visible.

text3DLesson.purposeBody: Flat text works well for labels, but has no solid sides when viewed from an angle. Text3D generates geometry from a font when a title should receive light, show depth or use 3D materials like a scene object.

purposeCards.title: Generate glyphs directly
purposeCards.body: Provide a font and string to create text geometry without modeling each title individually.

purposeCards.title: Use scene materials
purposeCards.body: The glyphs are meshes that can use materials and scene lighting; the actual result depends on both.

text3DLesson.demoLead: Observe depth and bevel from an angled view.
text3DLesson.demoBody: The example rotates DREI slightly and lights it; the panel controls font size, extrusion depth and bevel.

experiments.title: 01 · Increase depth
experiments.body: Reset and increase depth from 0.30 m. The sides of the letters grow wider while the font still defines the front outline.

experiments.title: 02 · Enable bevel
experiments.body: Toggle bevel and inspect the sloped edges and lighting changes. This example uses 0.04 for both bevel size and thickness.

experiments.title: 03 · Change size
experiments.body: Change font size to see the glyph dimensions change. Center recalculates the position when parameters change to aid comparison.

text3DLesson.parameterLead: Prepare a font, then adjust size, depth and edges.
text3DLesson.parameterNote: The installed drei 10.7.9 uses height for extrusion depth; higher subdivision usually produces more geometry.
parameters: Three.js font data or URL, not the same format as TTF / WOFF.
Extrusion depth; this version uses height.
Enables sloped edges; this demo sets bevelSize and bevelThickness to 0.04, distinct from the font size prop.
Subdivide bevels and glyph curves respectively; higher values can smooth outlines while adding geometry.
Adjust glyph spacing and line height.
Tolerance for vertex merging and normal recomputation.
text3DLesson.codeLead: Start with the minimal example, then connect the key code to the experiment.

codeNotes.title: 01 · Load the font
codeNotes.body: font points to Three.js typeface JSON; Suspense waits for the resource rather than passing a TTF directly to Text3D.

codeNotes.title: 02 · Extrude the letters
codeNotes.body: size controls font size, height controls depth and bevelEnabled adds an edge; bevel dimensions and subdivisions determine its shape.

codeNotes.title: 03 · Material and centering
codeNotes.body: meshStandardMaterial and scene lights create shading. Center uses a cacheKey that changes with demo parameters to recalculate centering.

text3DLesson.applicationsLead: Use when the letters themselves are a visual centerpiece.

applications.title: Exhibition or event titles
applications.body: Generate a small number of large entrance letters that need visible sides, materials and lighting.

applications.title: Configurable brand text
applications.body: Regenerate a short title when its wording changes instead of preparing a separate model for each version.

text3DLesson.boundariesLead: Consider geometry generation and rendering cost as text becomes more complex.

boundaries.title: Many frequently changing strings
boundaries.body: Changing long strings repeatedly regenerates geometry; consider flat Text or web DOM for ordinary labels and paragraphs.

boundaries.title: Font format and coverage
boundaries.body: Text3D needs compatible typeface JSON with the required outlines; this example font mainly covers Latin characters.

boundaries.title: Accessibility
boundaries.body: 3D glyphs are not native web text. Provide accessible DOM content for important titles or descriptions.

conceptDetails: Think of each letter as a shape cut from an outline: the font defines the front, then extrusion along a depth axis creates front, back and sides. Text3D renders that geometry as a scene mesh.
This demo starts with size 0.7 and height 0.3. Increasing height extends the extrusion; increasing size changes the overall glyph size. A bevel adds sloped edges whose shading depends on the lights.
The font input is Three.js typeface JSON, not a raw TTF. Its data must contain the required glyphs, and changes to the text require geometry to be regenerated.
purposeDetails: Flat Text is usually more direct for a description; an event title or shop sign needing real thickness, material and lighting needs actual geometry. Text3D converts font outlines into that geometry.
Extrusion and bevel add vertices and faces. Short titles can benefit from the effect; for many frequently changing strings compare flat Text or DOM for cost and accessibility.
codeDetails: font points to local typeface JSON and Suspense waits for loading. The Text3D child supplies the string, size sets font size, height sets extrusion depth, and meshStandardMaterial combines with scene directional lighting to produce shading.

The live experiment rotates the text group slightly to expose its sides. Center uses the bounding box; its cacheKey changes with size, depth and bevel so the example recalculates centering after geometry changes.

htmlUI.legend: Amber: label anchor · Indigo: occluder · units: meters
htmlUI.label: Scene label
htmlUI.hint: Move the occluder in front of the anchor and toggle occlusion; change anchor depth to compare label scale.

htmlLesson.conceptLead: Make a web element follow a position in a 3D scene.
htmlLesson.conceptBody: Html places React DOM content in a web container associated with the Canvas and updates it from a 3D anchor and camera. The label is an HTML element, not a 3D mesh rendered in the canvas.

conceptCards.title: 3D anchor
conceptCards.body: position is a scene coordinate. Html updates the on-screen label when the camera or anchor moves.

conceptCards.title: Web element
conceptCards.body: Children remain HTML and CSS and may contain text, buttons or forms; they do not automatically become 3D geometry.

conceptCards.title: Can only part of a label be hidden?
conceptCards.body: This demo raycasts to the anchor: if the box blocks it, the whole label is hidden rather than clipped to the box outline.

htmlLesson.purposeLead: Why not draw the text directly in the canvas?
htmlLesson.purposeBody: Scene meshes are useful for 3D rendering, but rich layout, forms and web controls require extra work. Html lets an existing React interface follow a scene position while retaining DOM layout, events and semantics.

purposeCards.title: Reuse web interfaces
purposeCards.body: Build product details or controls with familiar CSS and React components, then anchor them in the scene.

purposeCards.title: Connect camera and interface
purposeCards.body: The component updates the label as the camera moves, avoiding manual projection of scene coordinates on every frame.

htmlLesson.demoLead: Move the anchor and box to compare position and occlusion.
htmlLesson.demoBody: The orange sphere marks the label anchor; the indigo box is in front of it. The label uses transform, sprite and distanceFactor; this demo does not receive pointer events.

experiments.title: 01 · Follow the anchor
experiments.body: Reset and move anchor X: the orange marker and label move together, showing that the label follows scene coordinates.

experiments.title: 02 · Change distance
experiments.body: Reset and move anchor Z from −1 m to 0 m. The label moves closer and appears larger because this demo uses CSS 3D transforms and perspective.

experiments.title: 03 · Test occlusion

conceptDetails: Web elements and a WebGL canvas are drawn by different systems. A normal div above the canvas only knows page coordinates; it will not automatically follow a handle on a moving 3D product.

Html accepts a scene position as its anchor and updates the DOM presentation using the current camera. The label follows the camera and anchor while the browser still lays out its contents, so CSS, buttons and forms remain available.
Occlusion is a separate decision: this demo casts a ray from the camera to the anchor. If the chosen box blocks it, the whole label is hidden; it is not clipped along the box outline.
purposeDetails: A manual solution must project world coordinates to the screen and update the DOM when the camera, canvas or object moves; it also needs rules for objects behind the camera or occluded by others. Html brings common position synchronization and optional occlusion together.
For flat lettering rendered in WebGL, consider Text. For real web controls, selectable text or existing CSS layout, Html is a better fit. Many labels still incur DOM and occlusion-check costs.
codeDetails: The minimal example places Html inside Canvas with an ordinary div child. center applies to its non-transform mode; distanceFactor influences displayed size, whose exact effect also depends on mode and camera.

The live experiment uses position for the anchor and transform plus sprite for a camera-facing CSS 3D label. occlude receives the box ref, while pointerEvents="none" keeps the passive label from intercepting the pointer. useFrame updates the moving box world matrix before raycasting.

conceptDetails: ScreenQuad supplies a mesh covering the screen area. Despite its name, this version uses one oversized triangle with vertices (−1,−1), (3,−1), (−1,3), covering the visible clip region.
Coverage does not mean every material automatically bypasses the camera. This demo’s vertex shader writes position.xy directly to clip-space gl_Position, so camera distance does not change coverage.
The fragment shader computes colors from screen position; this example uses uBands for stripe frequency. Different shaders can produce entirely different results on the same geometry.
purposeDetails: Full-screen shaders, procedural backgrounds and post-processing need fragment calculations across the screen. ScreenQuad provides covering geometry so the material and shaders can handle the effect.
It is not a conventional world-space display panel and does not automatically create a post-processing pipeline. Use an ordinary Plane when camera projection should affect the surface.
codeDetails: The example vertex shader outputs clip-space coordinates directly and passes screen UV to the fragment shader; depthTest and depthWrite are disabled here.

The live demo updates uBands on the actual material instance. Changing camera Z does not affect the image because this vertex shader bypasses projection, not because ScreenQuad guarantees that for all materials.

conceptDetails: RoundedBox is a rounded-edge box mesh component combining rounded geometry and a mesh. Dimensions set the overall extent and radius controls edge rounding.
Rounding adds transition geometry rather than only changing material highlights. A larger radius expands the rounded region; dimensions and radius must be compatible to produce the intended shape.
bevelSegments controls subdivisions across the rounded transition. Fewer segments may look angular; more generally smooth the edge at additional geometry cost.
purposeDetails: Cards, buttons and soft-edged placeholders often need a gentler contour than Box. RoundedBox combines mesh, rounded geometry and a child material.
Choose RoundedBoxGeometry when only the geometry is needed for custom mesh composition; highly complex rounded products may need dedicated models.

conceptDetails: Tube samples a Three.js Curve, builds circular cross-sections around it and connects them into a tubular surface. The curve defines the centerline and radius defines thickness.
Imagine moving a circular ring along a path and joining neighboring cross-sections: when the path bends, the tube bends. Changing path controls does not directly change cross-section radius.
Path segments approximate the curve and radial segments approximate the cross-section. Too few can make bends angular or the cross-section polygonal, respectively.
purposeDetails: Cables, tubular trajectories and curved paths need thickness around an arbitrary route. Tube connects Curve and TubeGeometry to a declarative scene.
For a simple line, Line or a curve-line component is lighter; physics collision and closed end caps require separate handling.
codeDetails: Pass a Curve in args along with path segments, radius, radial segments and closure; the child material controls appearance.
The demo changes a Bézier control-point height. A pale centerline shows the path and the tube follows it; wireframe exposes path and cross-section sampling.

conceptDetails: A Torus resembles a tube bent into a ring. The major radius defines the circular path of the tube center, while the tube radius defines its cross-section; these are not inner and outer radii.

For major radius 1 m and tube radius 0.2 m, the outer edge is about 1.2 m from the center and the inner edge about 0.8 m. Increasing tube radius alone thickens the ring and reduces the central opening.
An arc smaller than a full revolution generates only part of the path. Segments control approximation along the ring and cross-section, both visible in wireframe.
purposeDetails: Tire-like decoration, handles and circular tracks can be described directly by two radii. Torus packages the tubular ring geometry and mesh for adjustment.
Ring is simpler for a flat annulus; Tube can generate a pipe along an arbitrary curve instead of a circular path.
codeDetails: The major and tube radii in args control the center path and cross-section; later segment and arc values control approximation and coverage.

conceptDetails: TorusKnot generates a tubular mesh along a torus-knot curve rather than decorating a normal ring. Integers p and q affect the route, while tube radius controls the cross-section around it.
Changing p and q changes how the path winds and can change crossings and the overall silhouette. They are not independent length values; radius and viewpoint also affect the visible result.
The tube is approximated by discrete segments along the path and cross-section. Too few look angular; more increase geometry cost.
purposeDetails: A torus knot can serve as an abstract sculpture, mathematical shape or visual focal point. TorusKnot generates the closed tubular form without manually implementing path equations and cross-section sampling.
Torus is simpler for a circular tube; Tube with a custom curve is preferable when the path comes from application control points.

conceptDetails: Polyhedron builds a polyhedron from vertex coordinates and triangle indices, then projects vertices onto a sphere of the chosen radius. Each three input numbers form an XYZ vertex; each three indices define a triangle.

conceptDetails: Extrude extends a 2D Shape along a depth axis to generate front, back and side surfaces; holes in the outline create through-hole sidewalls.
For example, adding depth to a planar sign makes thickness visible from the side. Increasing depth changes thickness, while hole radius changes the opening; they control different dimensions.
A bevel adds transition faces at edges; curve and bevel segments affect contour approximation and mesh density. It is not merely a lighting effect.
purposeDetails: Signs, parts and graphic marks with holes may need a solid appearance from a 2D path. Extrude connects Shape and extrusion geometry to a declarative mesh.
Shape is simpler for a flat area without thickness; manufacturing-accurate dimensions or complex Boolean topology need a suitable modeling workflow.
codeDetails: Pass a Three.js Shape and extrusion options to Extrude; depth sets extrusion and bevelEnabled with related props controls edge transitions.

conceptDetails: Cylinder creates a side surface along local Y with independently configurable top and bottom radii. Equal radii form a cylinder; different radii form a frustum; a zero radius at one end can form a cone.
Height is the distance between ends. Radial segments affect the circular silhouette and height segments add divisions along the side without changing either radius.
Caps can be removed to see inside. The demo uses a double-sided material for the interior, but a single surface does not have physical wall thickness.
purposeDetails: Bottles, pillars and frustums often need separate end radii. Cylinder packages the geometry and mesh as a declarative component.
Cone is more direct for a pointed top; use another modeling approach for inner and outer walls with real thickness.
codeDetails: args sets top radius, bottom radius, height, segments and whether caps are open. A child material controls surface appearance.
Adjust the ends and compare wireframe and cap settings: radii define cross-sections, segments define approximation and caps determine whether end faces exist.

conceptDetails: Circle is a disc in the local XY plane with its front facing +Z. Triangles connect its center to the circular boundary; it has no thickness and is not a sphere.
Radius controls disc size; start angle and angular extent choose where the arc begins and how much is drawn. Less than a full turn produces a sector, not solid side walls.
The arc is approximated by finite segments: fewer segments make a polygonal edge, while more approach a circle.
purposeDetails: Circular markers, sector progress and planar decorations need simple disc geometry. Circle combines mesh and CircleGeometry with adjustable radius and angles.
Use Ring for a hole in the middle; a disc cannot substitute for solid geometry when thickness or a spherical surface is required.
codeDetails: args contains radius, segment count, start angle and angular extent; a material attaches to the component mesh.

conceptDetails: Capsule consists of a central cylinder and two hemispheres along local Y. Radius sets both cylinder and hemisphere width; length is the straight middle section, not total height.
For radius 0.5 m and middle length 1 m, the two hemispheres add 1 m together, giving about 2 m overall height. Increasing length alone extends the middle without changing hemisphere radius.
The curved surface is approximated by a mesh. Fewer cap and radial segments look more angular; more can smooth the outline while adding vertices and faces.
purposeDetails: Capsule shapes are useful for character placeholders, pill-like buttons and simplified models. Capsule combines geometry and mesh without manually joining cylinders and hemispheres.
It is visual geometry and does not automatically create a physics collider; use a model or another geometry for complex precise outlines.

conceptDetails: Box is a convenience mesh for a rectangular solid: geometry defines the shape and the child material defines its surface appearance. Width, height and depth follow local X, Y and Z; mesh transforms determine scene position and rotation.
A 2 × 1 × 1 box is longer along X than the other axes. Changing width alters its geometric extent, while changing position translates it.
Segments on each axis determine face mesh density. More segments do not round a flat box, but provide vertices for later deformation; wireframe reveals the subdivisions.
purposeDetails: A manual box needs a mesh, BoxGeometry and a material. Box combines mesh and geometry for declarative placeholders and simple product shapes.
Consider RoundedBox for softened edges; complex real shapes need a model or custom geometry rather than simply more box segments.

The demo changes dimensions and shows subdivisions in wireframe. Dimensions change the boundary; segments primarily change triangle density.

conceptDetails: CurveModifier maps a child mesh near a curve, bending a model originally laid out along X. Think of laying a straight strip along a path rather than moving the whole rigid object onto it.
Flow performs deformation in a shader; the original mesh needs enough subdivisions or long edges have too few vertices to follow bends. Curve shape and offset along the curve are separate inputs.
The demo’s pale line is the reference path and the indigo strip is the deformed mesh. Path height changes the bend; offset moves the mesh along the path.
purposeDetails: Bending a road strip, text band or trim along a curve manually requires per-vertex transforms and path synchronization. CurveModifier connects Flow to the React scene.
It suits visual deformation along a path, not rigid-body movement, automatic collider updates or a guarantee against self-intersections.
codeDetails: Place a subdivided child mesh inside CurveModifier and supply a curve; offset controls its position along that path. Original mesh orientation and length affect the mapping.
The demo independently adjusts ellipse height and offset. The path line provides a reference for the deformed strip; fewer mesh subdivisions would make the bend approximation poorer.

conceptDetails: MarchingCubes maintains a 3D scalar field and extracts a mesh at a threshold. Imagine every position in space holding a value; the surface lies where values cross the chosen threshold.

MarchingCube and MarchingPlane children add contributions to that shared field. As two spherical fields approach, their contributions combine and the extracted isosurface may join; this is not a Boolean union of ordinary sphere meshes.
resolution controls field sampling density: lower values produce a coarser surface, while higher values can add detail at increased computation and geometry cost.
purposeDetails: A fused soft shape requires dynamically generating a surface from several contributions; separate sphere meshes do not naturally blend. The container manages the field, extraction and material together.
It suits visualization and soft-looking effects; it does not automatically provide accurate physics, collisions or fixed topology.
codeDetails: MarchingCubes wraps a material and field-source children; resolution controls sampling and isolation controls the surface threshold.

conceptDetails: MarchingCube is a child that adds a spherical contribution to a shared MarchingCubes scalar field; it is not an independent sphere mesh. The container extracts the final surface from all source contributions.

Distant sources may produce separate surfaces; as they approach, values combine and regions above the threshold can join. Changing strength alters the field contribution and therefore the contour and blend.
The container threshold, sampling density and other field sources also affect the result, so source parameters alone do not determine the final shape.
purposeDetails: Independent sphere meshes intersect without naturally producing a continuous blended surface. MarchingCube supplies a placeable spherical field source for the container’s combined mesh.
For a precise sphere, collider or fixed vertex topology, an ordinary Sphere or another modeling method is often more appropriate.
codeDetails: Place MarchingCube inside MarchingCubes; position and strength define its contribution and the container combines sources and extracts the surface.

conceptDetails: MarchingPlane adds an axis-oriented plane contribution to the shared MarchingCubes scalar field. It is a field source, not a separately created plane mesh with its own material.

Toggling the Y plane in this demo combines its contribution with two sphere sources and changes the isosurface extracted by the container. The visible surface is one generated mesh, not merely a plane mesh stacked with spheres.

purposeDetails: To create a continuous transition between a soft field and a directional base, add a plane contribution to the same scalar field instead of drawing an ordinary plane.

conceptDetails: Line renders an array of points as lines; it does not automatically create a smooth curve. By default it connects neighboring points in order; segments mode treats each pair as an independent line segment.
For points A, B, C and D, continuous mode draws A→B→C→D, whereas segment mode draws A→B and C→D without B→C. The points stay fixed while the connection rule changes.
The component uses Three.js wide-line implementations and exposes color, width and dashed styling. Dash spacing is presentation and does not change path points.
purposeDetails: Wide lines require appropriate geometry, material and resolution updates. Line integrates those objects with React Three Fiber’s component lifecycle for declarative changes.
It suits polylines, guides and outlines; choose a Bézier or Catmull-Rom component to sample a smooth parameterized path.
codeDetails: points supplies coordinates; segments selects independent pairs, while lineWidth and dashed control appearance.
The demo keeps four points fixed and changes connection mode, dashes and width. Whether B connects to C directly reveals the effect of segments.

conceptDetails: A Catmull-Rom spline interpolates a smooth curve through a set of path points, useful for describing a route through specified places. The ideal continuous curve passes through those points; a sparsely sampled displayed polyline may not.
Unlike Bézier handles, these points represent positions the curve should pass through. Moving one affects its neighboring curve; point spacing and interpolation type also affect the bend.
Closing connects the end back to the beginning. More segments improve the displayed approximation without changing path-point coordinates.
purposeDetails: For a route through several locations, placing Bézier handles for every segment and keeping joins smooth can be cumbersome. Catmull-Rom builds an interpolated curve directly from path points.
Bézier curves can be preferable when endpoint tangent control is essential; Line is sufficient when only straight connections are needed.
codeDetails: points supplies path positions, closed chooses whether to form a loop, curveType selects interpolation and segments controls visible sampling density.
Move the amber path points and switch closure or type. With fewer segments, compare the displayed line with the points to see the approximation differ from the ideal curve.

conceptDetails: A cubic Bézier curve uses a start, an end and two control points. Its initial direction runs from the start toward A, and its final direction runs from B toward the end; control points are not usually points on the curve.
Think of A and B as handles for the two ends: moving A primarily changes the start region and moving B primarily changes the end region, while both affect the entire curve.
The component samples the continuous curve into a polyline. Segment count affects the approximation, not the mathematical curve defined by the controls.
purposeDetails: When one control point cannot independently adjust both endpoint tangents, a cubic curve offers more freedom for paths, connections and smooth transitions.
The component packages sampling and line rendering; CatmullRomLine can be more direct when the curve should pass through several specified positions.
codeDetails: start and end are endpoints, midA and midB are control points; segments controls sampling and line props control appearance.
The demo moves A and B independently to compare the ends, then reduces segments to reveal the polyline approximation. Control points describe shape, not objects moving along the curve.

conceptDetails: A quadratic Bézier curve is defined by a start, an end and one control point. Treat the control point as a handle that pulls the curve: moving it changes the direction and amount of bending, but the curve generally does not pass through it.

Near the start the curve heads toward the control point; near the end it arrives along the direction from control point to end. With the control point on the endpoints’ line, the curve lies along that line.
The displayed line is a polyline sampled from a continuous curve. Fewer segments expose corners; more segments generally look smoother but require more line segments.
purposeDetails: A simple arc between two points often needs to respond to an editable handle. A manual implementation constructs the curve, samples it and manages line geometry; QuadraticBezierLine packages that workflow.
One control point suits simple bends. Compare CubicBezierLine to adjust the two ends independently or CatmullRomLine to pass through several specified positions.
codeDetails: start and end define endpoints, mid defines the control point, and segments controls sampling. The component samples the curve into a visible line.
The demo sliders move the control point in X/Y while endpoints stay fixed. Fewer segments do not change the mathematical curve, but make the displayed approximation coarser.

perspectiveLesson.conceptLead: Project a three-dimensional world onto a flat image.
perspectiveLesson.conceptBody: PerspectiveCamera wraps the Three.js perspective camera in a React component. Equal-sized objects appear smaller farther away, and parallel lines appear to converge. It controls how you see the scene, rather than moving objects.

conceptCards.title: Field of view
conceptCards.body: The vertical viewing angle in degrees. At a fixed position, a wider angle captures more of the scene.

conceptCards.title: View frustum
conceptCards.body: The visible volume is a truncated pyramid, defined by FOV, aspect ratio and clipping planes.

conceptCards.title: Projection and controls
conceptCards.body: The camera defines projection. Controls such as OrbitControls manipulate the camera. They can work together.

perspectiveLesson.purposeLead: Canvas already has a camera. Why add this one?
perspectiveLesson.purposeBody: R3F Canvas provides a perspective camera by default. Its camera prop is sufficient for simple scenes. A separate component helps when cameras belong to scene lifecycles, need to become the default, or have attached children.

purposeCards.title: Declare a camera
purposeCards.body: Describe it in JSX. Parameters follow React state, while mounting and cleanup follow the component lifecycle.

purposeCards.title: Follow the canvas
purposeCards.body: By default, drei updates aspect and the projection matrix with canvas dimensions to avoid stretched images.

purposeCards.title: Take over the view
purposeCards.body: makeDefault registers this camera with R3F. Unmounting restores the previous camera. Creating a camera alone does not activate it.

perspectiveLesson.demoLead: Three equal cubes. Three different apparent sizes.
perspectiveLesson.demoBody: Each cube is 1 meter across, at z = 2, −2 and −6. The camera looks down −Z. Predict the result before adjusting the controls.

experiments.title: 01 · Change FOV
experiments.body: Reset, then change FOV from 50° to 90°. More of the scene fits and the cubes shrink. The camera has not moved, so their relative perspective size relationship stays the same.

experiments.title: 02 · Move away
experiments.body: Reset, then change distance from 8 m to 16 m. All cubes shrink, and the relative size difference between near and far cubes decreases.

experiments.title: 03 · Clip space
experiments.body: Reset and increase near to 7 m to clip the closest cube. Reset again and decrease far to 13 m to hide the farthest cube. Clipping does not delete the objects.

perspectiveLesson.parameterLead: Library defaults and demonstration values are different.
perspectiveLesson.parameterNote: These are the core parameters and drei-specific capabilities used in this lesson. position and zoom come from Three.js. distance is a control in this demo that changes position.z, not a camera prop.
parameters: Use this camera to render Canvas; restore the previous camera on unmount.
Vertical viewing angle. Larger values capture more at a fixed position; this is not horizontal FOV.
World coordinates in meters. Only z changes here; without lookAt the camera keeps facing −Z.
Clipping planes must satisfy 0 < near < far. Avoid an unnecessarily large depth range.
Updated by drei by default; determines horizontal framing, rather than CSS dimensions.
Scales the projection and affects effective FOV without moving the camera.
Manage aspect yourself. Imperative property changes require a projection matrix update.
Regular children follow the camera; function children receive an offscreen texture.
Offscreen target resolution in function-children mode, not main canvas resolution.
Offscreen frame count in function-children mode. The installed 10.7.9 implementation renders continuously by default.
Temporarily sets the scene background for offscreen rendering; does not configure main scene environment lighting.
perspectiveLesson.codeLead: Start with the smallest example, then connect it to the experiment.

codeNotes.title: 01 · makeDefault
codeNotes.body: Activate this camera for rendering. Without it, Canvas generally continues using its own default camera.

codeNotes.title: 02 · State becomes props
codeNotes.body: Zustand stores FOV, distance, near and far. Sliders update state; the scene reads it and updates camera props.

codeNotes.title: 03 · Fix the scene, compare projection
codeNotes.body: Cube dimensions and positions stay unchanged. The code reflects current camera values; paste it inside an existing Canvas to reproduce the camera setup.

perspectiveLesson.applicationsLead: Use it when depth and a natural spatial view matter.

applications.title: Product configurators
applications.body: Present furniture, clothing or vehicles in 3D, combining OrbitControls for inspection. Adjust FOV and distance for framing.

applications.title: Architectural walkthroughs
applications.body: Convey scale and depth in virtual spaces. Add first-person controls, with separate collision and movement handling.

applications.title: Games and narrative cameras
applications.body: Build first-person, third-person and cinematic views. Camera components manage projection; controls or animations handle movement.

perspectiveLesson.boundariesLead: Choose a projection that serves the spatial task.

boundaries.title: Precise size comparisons
boundaries.body: Perspective shrinks distant objects. Plans, isometric views and engineering editors often benefit from OrthographicCamera.

boundaries.title: Fixed-pixel interfaces
boundaries.body: Use DOM for ordinary buttons, tables and dashboards. Consider Html or Hud for scene overlays; a camera does not replace interface layout.

boundaries.title: Automatic interaction or collision
boundaries.body: PerspectiveCamera does not provide dragging, navigation or collision. Combine it with OrbitControls, CameraControls or a physics system.

conceptDetails: Perspective projection resembles viewing from one point: equal-sized objects occupy less of the image as they move farther from the camera. Their world dimensions remain unchanged; only their apparent size from this viewpoint changes.

FOV is the vertical viewing angle. With a fixed camera position, a wider FOV includes more of the scene but makes the same object occupy less of the image. Moving the camera also changes relative distances and perspective relationships.
near and far are clipping distances along the viewing direction, not object dimensions. The region between them defines visible depth; objects outside it remain in the scene even when not rendered.
purposeDetails: Canvas already supplies a perspective camera, so fixed views can be configured directly with its camera prop. A declared PerspectiveCamera is useful when managing or replacing cameras in the component tree, responding to canvas size, or attaching children to a camera.

Creating a second camera alone does not change the view. makeDefault installs it as the current R3F camera and restores the previous one on unmount. A camera controller moves or rotates the camera; it is distinct from the projection type.
codeDetails: The minimal example declares a camera inside Canvas and uses makeDefault to select it. position is a 3D location and fov is the vertical angle; a newly created camera faces its local −Z direction by default.

The live experiment maps the distance control to the z component of position rather than moving the objects. FOV affects framing, while near and far affect visible depth; compare the boxes to distinguish them.

orthographicLesson.conceptLead: Distance changes. Projected size stays the same.
orthographicLesson.conceptBody: OrthographicCamera projects along parallel rays. Equally sized and oriented objects keep the same projected size at different distances. Depth, occlusion and clipping still exist; perspective scaling does not.

conceptCards.title: Parallel projection
conceptCards.body: Moving along the viewing axis does not scale objects. Change zoom or frustum bounds instead.

conceptCards.title: Screen scale
conceptCards.body: With drei’s canvas-sized bounds, zoom=65 projects 1 meter to approximately 65 CSS pixels.

conceptCards.title: Depth remains
conceptCards.body: Near objects can occlude far objects, and the far plane still clips distant geometry.

orthographicLesson.purposeLead: When size comparison matters more than natural perspective.
orthographicLesson.purposeBody: Editors, plans and isometric games need stable size relationships. Drei declares the camera as a component, supplies canvas-sized frustum bounds and manages default-camera activation.

purposeCards.title: Stable ratios
purposeCards.body: Equal dimensions project equally, aiding alignment and comparison.

purposeCards.title: Declarative resizing
purposeCards.body: Mount a JSX camera with makeDefault; default bounds follow canvas dimensions.

purposeCards.title: Compose controls
purposeCards.body: Combine with controls such as MapControls for panning and zooming.

orthographicLesson.demoLead: The same three cubes, through a different projection.
orthographicLesson.demoBody: The 1-meter cubes sit at z=2, −2 and −6. The camera sits at [0, 0, distance] and faces −Z. Toggle perspective for comparison; the zoom control only affects orthographic mode.

experiments.title: 01 · Move back
experiments.body: Reset and change distance from 8 to 16. Cube sizes remain constant. Repeat in perspective mode to see distance scaling.

experiments.title: 02 · Scale projection
experiments.body: Reset and increase zoom from 65 to 100. All cubes grow equally, preserving their size ratios.

experiments.title: 03 · Clip depth
experiments.body: Reset and set near to 7 to clip the nearest cube. The far plane still clips distant objects.

orthographicLesson.parameterLead: No FOV: framing comes from bounds and zoom.
orthographicLesson.parameterNote: Defaults refer to installed drei 10.7.9. distance changes position.z and is not a camera prop. With default bounds, a wider canvas shows more horizontal world space.
parameters: Activate this camera and restore the previous one on unmount.
Positive projection scale; larger values enlarge objects.
Horizontal bounds default to half the canvas width.
Vertical bounds; explicit world-space bounds need aspect handling.
Moving along the view direction affects clipping, not size.
Orthographic near can be 0; near must be below far. The perspective comparison clamps 0 to 0.01.
Manage custom bounds and projection yourself; this is not automatic framing.
Supports the same function-child offscreen rendering API as PerspectiveCamera.
orthographicLesson.codeLead: Set scale with zoom and viewpoint with position.

codeNotes.title: 01 · Pixel bounds
codeNotes.body: Drei derives omitted bounds from canvas dimensions; no aspect prop is required.

codeNotes.title: 02 · Switch projection
codeNotes.body: Only one camera is mounted; makeDefault activates it. Perspective mode uses a fixed 50° FOV.

codeNotes.title: 03 · Two kinds of change
codeNotes.body: Moving back only changes position. Orthographic scaling requires zoom or bounds changes.

orthographicLesson.applicationsLead: For alignment, scale relationships and structural clarity.

applications.title: Engineering editors
applications.body: Plans, layout tools and dimension comparisons without depth-dependent size changes.

applications.title: Isometric games
applications.body: Combine with a fixed angled viewpoint for consistent board, building and character scale.

applications.title: Data and structure
applications.body: Charts, graphs and model sections where perspective would interfere with scale interpretation.

orthographicLesson.boundariesLead: Stable dimensions trade away natural perspective depth.

boundaries.title: Realistic walkthroughs
boundaries.body: Use PerspectiveCamera for interiors and first-person games that need natural depth scaling.

boundaries.title: Distance-based zoom
boundaries.body: Moving away does not widen orthographic framing; change zoom or use perspective.

boundaries.title: Ordinary interfaces
boundaries.body: Orthographic projection does not make WebGL necessary for ordinary DOM forms and lists.

conceptDetails: Orthographic projection uses parallel projection directions, so an object does not shrink on screen merely because it is farther from the camera. The three one-meter boxes in this demo have equal projected size at different depths when oriented alike.
Depth still matters: a nearer object can occlude a farther one, and near and far clip content outside the visible range. Moving the camera can also change which objects lie within that range.
zoom changes the projection scale of the visible area. Increasing this demo from 65 to 100 enlarges all boxes together rather than making the nearest one larger relative to the farthest.
purposeDetails: When comparing dimensions or editing a plan, perspective size changes can make judgment harder. Orthographic projection keeps equal sizes at a consistent screen scale; perspective may be preferable for presentations that emphasize depth.
The drei component declares the camera in React and can make it the default; by default it updates its bounds from the canvas size. It defines projection, not drag or zoom input by itself.
codeDetails: Declare OrthographicCamera inside Canvas and set makeDefault to use it as the rendering camera. position sets the viewpoint and zoom adjusts projection scale.

The experiment also provides a perspective comparison. Move each camera and observe the one-meter boxes to contrast fixed orthographic size with perspective distance changes. near and far control depth clipping in both.

orthoControls.hint: In orthographic mode, moving back preserves size; increasing zoom enlarges objects.
orthoControls.label: Orthographic and perspective comparison

conceptDetails: A cube environment texture contains six images facing different directions. CubeCamera captures the surrounding scene in six directions from one position; the material samples that texture by direction to create environmental reflections.

It is not the main camera used to view the page. Moving the main camera changes the viewpoint; updating the six-direction capture is required for moving objects to appear at their latest positions in the reflection.
The demo uses a metallic sphere and recognizable moving objects. Higher roughness blurs reflected detail; capture resolution determines the pixel dimensions of each cube face.
purposeDetails: A static environment map is useful for reflections that do not need scene updates, but it does not automatically contain moving objects. A manual dynamic solution needs a cube render target, six-direction updates and self-reflection handling.

CubeCamera packages that workflow and temporarily hides its children during capture so a reflective object does not capture itself. Live updates render six directions, so less frequent updates can be appropriate for static content.
codeDetails: The function child receives the captured texture and the example passes it to the sphere material’s envMap. CubeCamera position determines where the surrounding scene is captured.

The demo contrasts live and frozen updates: scene objects continue moving when frozen, while the texture keeps its previous capture until refreshed. Material roughness and capture resolution independently affect blur and captured detail.

conceptDetails: useCubeCamera provides a cube camera, a render target fbo and an update function. Calling update captures six directions from the capture position; fbo.texture holds the result for a material’s environment map.

The main camera controls the user’s view; the cube camera captures the reflection environment. Changing the main view does not refresh that texture. After a scene object moves, another update is needed to capture its new position.

The hook does not schedule updates or exclude the reflective object automatically. The caller chooses when to capture and, if needed, temporarily hides the target to prevent it from appearing in its own environment texture.
purposeDetails: The component form suits conventional capture and hides its children automatically. When updates should occur only after an object moves, a scene changes or a particular frame arrives, the hook gives the caller control over timing and included objects.
Each update renders six directions. Reducing frequency can reduce work but leaves reflections showing an older state between captures, so the tradeoff depends on the scene.
codeDetails: Call useCubeCamera to create the camera and render target, then pass fbo.texture to the material’s envMap. update performs a capture; creating the texture alone does not keep it current.

The example hides the sphere before capture, calls update and restores visibility. Live mode repeats this process; frozen mode keeps the existing texture until the capture button requests another update.

conceptDetails: A device orientation sensor reports angles describing the device’s pose. DeviceOrientationControls converts them into camera rotation so turning or tilting the device changes the view without moving the camera position.

Device coordinates, screen orientation and Three.js camera coordinates differ. Directly assigning the three angles to camera rotation can produce incorrect orientation; the controller accounts for device and screen orientation.
This page first previews pose with sliders: beta=90° is its upright-device reference. Simulated values help explain directions but are not live sensor readings.
purposeDetails: Panorama viewing needs a mapping from handheld orientation to camera orientation. The controller handles angle conversion and frame updates; the page still handles permission, unsupported devices and missing data.

Sensor access depends on browser, device and secure context, and some platforms require a user gesture. Offer an alternative input when data is unavailable rather than presenting preview values as measurements.
codeDetails: The minimal example requests permission after user action and mounts DeviceOrientationControls only when allowed; makeDefault registers it as the current controller.

conceptDetails: FlyControls moves and rotates a free camera without orbiting a fixed target. Forward, sideways and vertical movement change position; pitch, yaw and roll change orientation.

Movement follows the camera’s local axes. Rolling with Q/E tilts the horizon; pressing W afterward still moves in the camera’s current forward direction rather than automatically following a level floor.
It does not provide gravity, ground constraints or collision. A character that must stop at walls needs those rules elsewhere in the application.
purposeDetails: Free exploration needs continuous keyboard and mouse input, frame-time-based position and rotation updates, and combined input handling. FlyControls provides those basics and drei connects it to the frame loop.
OrbitControls is more intuitive for orbiting a product without moving through the scene; ground-based character navigation additionally needs character controls, collision and gravity.

conceptDetails: MapControls uses a camera orbit around a target but maps input to familiar map gestures: left drag pans, right drag rotates and the wheel changes distance in this demo. It controls a camera; it does not load maps or convert geographic coordinates.

Left-drag panning moves both camera and target, changing the observation center. Right-drag rotation changes the camera angle around the current target. The orange marker and panel coordinates distinguish the two.
By default panning occurs in a plane perpendicular to camera up. In a Y-up scene that generally means movement along the ground rather than vertical movement on screen.
purposeDetails: In maps and floor plans, users often drag the ground to find a location before rotating their view. MapControls uses orbit logic with input mapping that supports this workflow.
OrbitControls may be preferable when left drag should rotate a product. In either case the application remains responsible for map tiles, coordinate systems and geographic positioning.

conceptDetails: Imagine a camera on an orbit around a product, always looking at a target. Dragging rotates the camera around that point and the wheel changes its distance; the model itself does not rotate.
Panning differs from orbiting: it moves both the camera and target, changing the observation center. The orange marker shows target and the panel reports camera and target coordinates.
OrbitControls constrains the camera’s up direction to help maintain a stable horizon; it is not a free-rolling flight controller.
purposeDetails: Handling pointer movement manually requires converting deltas into angles around a target while maintaining distance limits, pan direction and damping. OrbitControls combines these interactions and state.

The drei wrapper connects the controller to the camera and render loop and cleans it up on unmount. Consider MapControls for map-style left-button panning, or TrackballControls for free camera rotation.
codeDetails: Place OrbitControls inside Canvas to connect it to the current camera; target sets the orbit center, while distance and polar-angle limits constrain reachable views.

conceptDetails: TrackballControls lets the camera rotate freely around a target like a virtual trackball. Dragging changes camera position and orientation while the model and world axes stay still.

Unlike OrbitControls with a fixed up constraint, Trackball can pass over the top and change the camera up vector; the view can tilt or flip. It suits inspection of objects without a fixed upright direction.
With inertia enabled motion continues and decays after release; without it motion stops when input ends. The demo axes and up readout expose the orientation change.
purposeDetails: Manual free rotation requires accumulating camera orientation, moving around a target and handling motion decay after dragging. TrackballControls supplies those input behaviors.
OrbitControls is easier when a stable horizon or limited vertical angle is required; Trackball offers more freedom for inspecting molecules or mechanical parts.
codeDetails: TrackballControls connects to the current camera and operates around target. Rotation, zoom and pan can be enabled independently; maximum distance limits how far the camera can move from the target.

purposeDetails: When inspecting a complex model, users may rotate the whole object and then focus on a surface detail. Arcball combines spherical rotation and focusing in one controller rather than requiring manual target and camera management.

conceptDetails: CameraControls handles user orbit, pan and zoom as well as programmatic camera commands. It maintains camera position, target and transition state.

For example, a front-view button requests a new camera position and target. With smoothing the controller transitions over frames; without it the view changes immediately. fitToBox calculates framing from a bounding box and viewport.
User dragging and button commands affect the same controller, avoiding conflicts between controller updates and direct changes to camera.position.
purposeDetails: A product viewer may need both drag interaction and buttons such as “front” or “show all.” Combining orbit input, camera animation and target synchronization manually can lead to conflicting state; CameraControls provides one control interface.
OrbitControls can be enough for basic orbiting. CameraControls instance methods are useful for business-driven smooth transitions and automatic framing.
codeDetails: Access the controller through a ref; setLookAt specifies position and target, and fitToBox frames an object’s bounding box. The transition argument decides whether a command animates.
