conceptDetails: CameraControlsImpl is the underlying camera-controls class, not a JSX component. It exposes the same control capabilities as the CameraControls wrapper, but the caller owns construction, input connection and lifecycle.
The instance holds camera, target and transition state. After commands such as setLookAt or fitToBox, the render loop must call update(delta) for smooth transitions to advance over time.
Dispose of the instance when finished to release listeners and related resources; otherwise navigation or repeated construction can leave extra input listeners.
purposeDetails: For ordinary React Three Fiber pages, the CameraControls component already manages integration and lifecycle. Use the underlying class for a custom render loop, non-React integration or instance extensions.
The additional flexibility carries responsibilities: install the Three.js dependency, bind DOM input, update every frame and dispose correctly.
codeDetails: The example first calls CameraControlsImpl.install({ THREE }), then creates an instance for the camera and DOM element; useFrame passes each frame delta to update.
On unmount it calls dispose. The demo uses the same presets and framing actions to show the underlying instance while its code makes creation, updating and cleanup explicit.

conceptDetails: For picking, R3F normally casts a ray through the pointer using its default camera and checks intersections with scene objects. If another camera renders the image, the ray for the same screen position can differ.

This demo renders using an orthographic camera offset horizontally, while the default camera has no matching offset. When C appears at screen center, a ray calculated with the default camera can hit B instead.
useCamera returns a function suitable for mesh.raycast so that object uses a specified camera for picking. It does not switch the main camera, move objects or change the rendered image.
purposeDetails: A multi-view or custom render can display an image with a camera different from R3F’s default picking camera. A specified camera can be used for meshes that need their picks to match that view.

When rendering and events already use the same default camera, useCamera is usually unnecessary. It does not replace complete multi-viewport event-coordinate management; the view layout still needs correct configuration.
codeDetails: Prepare customCamera, call useCamera(customCamera) to obtain raycast and pass it to the target mesh. The code also updates camera matrices so the ray uses current transforms.

The demo switch changes only the mesh raycast calculation, not the rendering camera. Compare hits at the same screen position with it on and off to see the effect of mismatched view and picking cameras.

cycleRaycastLesson.conceptLead: Cycle event intersections for overlapping objects.
cycleRaycastLesson.conceptBody: CycleRaycast reorders R3F ray intersections so objects behind a foreground hit can receive events. It does not alter geometry or camera position.

conceptCards.title: Ray intersections
conceptCards.body: R3F computes the hit list, normally sorted by distance.

conceptCards.title: Event order
conceptCards.body: Cycling changes event dispatch order, not rendering order.

conceptCards.title: Propagation
conceptCards.body: Calling stopPropagation on the target prevents the event continuing to later hits.

cycleRaycastLesson.purposeLead: Overlapping parts can hide the intended event target.
cycleRaycastLesson.purposeBody: R3F events normally follow intersection order. Cycling reorders the list and refreshes pointer events; stopPropagation can restrict the click to the current target.

purposeCards.title: Overlapping objects
purposeCards.body: Users may need to access parts behind other geometry or layers.

purposeCards.title: Preserve the view
purposeCards.body: Cycling hit order lets users switch targets without separating the model.

codeNotes.title: 01 · Hits
codeNotes.body: Pointer handlers make the planes eligible for move raycasts; the controller records intersections and resets the cycle when they change.

codeNotes.title: 02 · Cycle

conceptDetails: A ray through the pointer can intersect several objects. R3F obtains a list of intersections and normally handles nearer objects first; a foreground handler that stops propagation can prevent objects behind it from receiving the click.
CycleRaycast changes intersection event order so other hits at the same position can become the current target. It changes interaction targeting, not geometry, opacity or visibility.
This demo overlaps three planes in depth. After focusing the canvas and moving the pointer over them, press C to cycle targets, then click the same position and compare the panel’s target and result.
purposeDetails: An editor may need to select an object hidden behind another. Hiding or moving objects interrupts the workflow; cycling the hit order provides another way to reach candidates.
It suits selection tools with overlapping objects, not occlusion removal or camera projection. The application still needs to show the current target and manage focus and propagation.
codeDetails: CycleRaycast accepts a keyCode and callback; this demo uses C and disables wheel cycling. Pointer handlers make objects eligible for events, and click handlers use stopPropagation to prevent later objects handling the same click.

The example enables cycling while the canvas is focused and waits for a pointer move over it before allowing C. The panel records target changes and clicks; typing elsewhere should not cycle scene targets.

useCursorLesson.conceptLead: Set a container’s CSS cursor from hover state.
useCursorLesson.conceptBody: useCursor is a DOM hook that sets a cursor while hovered and restores the configured exit style on cleanup. It does not perform raycasting.

conceptCards.title: Hover state
conceptCards.body: Application code or R3F pointer events provide the boolean; the hook does not perform picking.

conceptCards.title: CSS cursor
conceptCards.body: While hovered, the hook writes a cursor style to the specified DOM element.

conceptCards.title: Exit style
conceptCards.body: On hover end or unmount, it writes the specified exit style rather than remembering the prior value.

useCursorLesson.purposeLead: Make interactive objects recognizable through pointer feedback.
useCursorLesson.purposeBody: R3F pointer events detect hover; the hook changes CSS cursor. Scoping the container to canvas avoids affecting the entire page.

purposeCards.title: Interaction cue
purposeCards.body: A pointer cursor helps users discover that a model is clickable.

purposeCards.title: Limit scope
purposeCards.body: Specifying the canvas instead of the default body confines the visual change.

useCursorLesson.demoBody: Hovering the cube changes the canvas cursor to pointer; the panel reads the canvas cursor style and hover state. Clicking records a hit; leaving or unmounting restores the cursor.

experiments.title: 02 · Restore on exit

conceptDetails: useCursor sets the CSS cursor on a DOM element from a boolean state, for example pointer while hovered and auto after leaving. It changes the browser pointer’s appearance, not a 3D object’s position.
The hook does not determine whether the pointer intersects a mesh. The example uses R3F onPointerOver and onPointerOut to update hovered and passes that state to useCursor.
The supplied DOM element determines the cursor’s scope. This example passes the canvas so moving elsewhere does not change the whole page cursor.
purposeDetails: Manually setting and restoring style.cursor across pointer events can miss state changes or unmount cleanup. useCursor connects hovered state to entry and exit styles.
It provides lightweight feedback for clickable scene objects, but pointer is only a visual cue. Click behavior, keyboard access and accessible names still belong to the application.
codeDetails: useThree obtains the renderer canvas; useCursor(hovered, pointer, auto, canvas) limits the cursor to it. Pointer events update hovered when entering or leaving the cube.
The cube color and click count are separate page state; useCursor controls only the cursor style. Compare hover, exit and click to distinguish those responsibilities.

conceptDetails: Dragging a 3D object starts with a 2D screen pointer. DragControls calculates movement from the intersection of the camera ray and a drag plane, then represents the result as a transformation matrix.
Here axisLock="z" means the drag plane has a Z normal: the cube moves in XY while Z remains fixed. It does not mean movement is restricted to the Z axis.
With autoTransform enabled, the controller applies the matrix; when disabled, application code handles the callback result. This demo copies the matrix in onDrag, so the cube still moves.
purposeDetails: Manual dragging requires a start position, ray-plane intersection, drag offset, constraints and coordination with camera controls. DragControls supplies those calculations and callbacks.
It suits planar arrangement and simple dragging, not full physics collision or constraint solving. For rotation and scale handles compare TransformControls or PivotControls.
codeDetails: The component wraps the cube and axisLock="z" selects the XY drag plane; dragLimits constrain each axis, here X/Y from −1.4 to 1.4 meters.
onDrag receives a local matrix. With autoTransform off, the demo copies it in the callback to update the scene; without applying the result, a controlled drag will not automatically move the object.

conceptDetails: A web scrollbar and a WebGL scene are different systems. ScrollControls creates an HTML scrolling container associated with Canvas and converts its position into progress readable by the scene.

The controller damps progress after the raw scroll position changes. The panel’s target progress and offset can differ temporarily; after scrolling stops, offset approaches the target and delta approaches zero.
The controller supplies input and shared state, not a fixed movement for every object. Scroll can translate content from progress, while useScroll lets the application calculate its own animation.
purposeDetails: Driving 3D animation from ordinary page scrolling requires synchronizing a DOM container, normalized progress and R3F events. ScrollControls combines that infrastructure.

It suits experiences where scrolling is part of the scene; an ordinary article does not necessarily need a canvas-owned scroll container. Accessibility and touch behavior still require validation in the actual layout.
codeDetails: Wrap consumers in ScrollControls; pages controls the scrolling length and damping affects how quickly offset follows input.
This example shares one progress value among 3D Scroll, HTML Scroll and the useScroll panel. Switching direction changes the scroll axis, while interval readouts show the damped offset.

conceptDetails: Scroll is a content container within ScrollControls. It reads shared scroll state and translates its children: the default mode moves a 3D group and html mode moves a web element layer.
Place moving objects inside Scroll and leave fixed background outside. In this demo a cube and an HTML label use the two Scroll modes with one shared progress value.
The scroll container receives input and Scroll moves content. Creating the controller alone does not automatically move every scene object, nor must every object use Scroll.
purposeDetails: In scroll storytelling, some elements should leave the view while background elements remain fixed. Scroll supplies a declarative boundary between them.
For opacity, rotation or complex paths driven by progress, useScroll supplies data for an application-defined mapping; Scroll translation is not a replacement for every animation.
codeDetails: Place <Scroll> around 3D objects inside ScrollControls; <Scroll html> carries HTML content. Objects outside those wrappers do not follow Scroll translation.
The panel displays useScroll offset while the cube and label move. Horizontal mode changes the scrolling and content movement direction.

conceptCards.title: range

conceptCards.title: curve / visible

conceptDetails: useScroll reads shared data from ScrollControls. offset is damped normalized progress and delta indicates progress change; they update per frame rather than being ordinary React state that necessarily rerenders on every scroll.
For an animation limited to 0.25–0.75, range(0.25, 0.5) maps that interval to local progress from 0 to 1, holding boundary values outside it.

curve rises then falls within the interval, while visible tests whether the offset is inside it. They answer different questions about the same offset: local progress, proximity to the middle and interval visibility.
purposeDetails: If each object separately calculates scroll intervals, clamping and boundary checks, animation logic is easily duplicated. useScroll provides current progress and interval helpers to consumers inside the controller.
It must be used inside ScrollControls. Scroll is useful for translating children directly; useScroll lets an application map progress to rotation, opacity or custom effects.
codeDetails: Call useScroll in a ScrollControls child, then read offset or call range, curve and visible in useFrame and update scene objects from the current frame result.
The demo interval starts at 0.25 and has length 0.5. Near offset 0.5, range is about 0.5 and curve is near its peak; displayed values follow damped offset rather than the instantaneous target.

conceptDetails: Keyboard hardware reports key presses and releases, while application logic often cares about named actions such as forward or left. KeyboardControls maps one or more keys to named boolean states and provides them through context.
The component manages input state; it does not move scene objects. Application code decides direction, speed and boundaries and whether diagonal movement should be normalized.
This demo scopes events to a focusable scene area. Leaving the canvas or typing in search should not continue to drive the scene.
purposeDetails: If each object listens for keydown and keyup independently, mappings, release state and listener cleanup are easily duplicated. KeyboardControls supplies shared action state to its children.
It suits components sharing a set of actions, but provides neither collision nor character physics or a complete focus strategy. The page still needs to make keyboard focus clear.
codeDetails: map binds keys to actions and KeyboardControls wraps the consumers; the event target determines the listening scope.
The example consumer reads action state and updates cube position per frame. The panel shows actions and coordinates; changing color while W is pressed is application feedback.

conceptDetails: useKeyboardControls reads named actions from the nearest KeyboardControls context. It does not create keyboard listeners or define mappings and must be used within that provider.

purposeDetails: After a controller centralizes input, consumers may need different access patterns: UI can react to selected state while per-frame movement may read a current snapshot.

conceptDetails: MotionPathControls treats one or more curves as a path and maps target progress to a position. Without object it controls the current camera; another scene object can be supplied.
current is desired progress and offset is the damped actual progress. When the target changes abruptly, the object can approach it gradually rather than jumping immediately.

The path point is the current position and the tangent describes curve direction at that point. Final orientation also depends on the look-at configuration, so tangent is not automatically identical to camera direction.
purposeDetails: A camera tour or moving exhibit needs business progress converted to a curve position with transitions and orientation. MotionPathControls handles sampling and movement while application logic chooses progress.
Free-moving characters or routes requiring collision avoidance need other control logic; a curve does not automatically plan navigation or handle physics collisions.
codeDetails: Provide curves to the controller, specify object or use the default camera, then change target progress through context. Damping makes actual offset follow the target.
The demo offers automatic or manual progress, looping and look-at options; the panel reports actual point, tangent and orientation for comparison.

conceptDetails: useMotion reads shared motion state from MotionPathControls. current is target progress and offset is the damped actual progress; a difference means the object is still approaching the target.
point is the current path position and tangent is the path direction there. These mutable values update during motion and do not imply a React rerender on every frame.
For example, when target progress changes to 1, offset can rise gradually from a lower value. Observing point and tangent as offset changes connects curve sampling to damping.
purposeDetails: Several components may need the same position, direction or progress along a path. useMotion provides controller context instead of requiring each consumer to sample the curve separately.
The hook neither creates a path nor decides when a user changes progress. It requires MotionPathControls context; the application still designs input and display updates.

conceptDetails: TransformControls shows a 3D gizmo around an object: axes, planes and rotation rings map drags to position, rotation or scale changes. It can attach to a specified object or wrap children.
Dragging handles changes the object transform. The demo reports local position, Euler rotation and scale; choosing world or local space changes the orientation of operation axes.
Snapping changes transforms in increments for alignment. It is not collision detection and does not automatically save edits or implement undo.
purposeDetails: A 3D editor needs constrained movement along an axis or rotation around a direction; an unconstrained screen drag does not express these operations clearly. TransformControls provides common gizmos and modes.
DragControls may be simpler for planar movement; compare PivotControls when adjustable pivot placement and matrix callbacks are required.

conceptDetails: PivotControls provides translation axes, planes, rotation arcs and scale handles with an adjustable pivot. The pivot is the reference point for a transform and need not be the geometry center.

For example, a door’s geometry center lies in the middle but it should rotate around a hinge at the edge. Place the pivot at that edge and dragging the rotation arc turns the door around that reference.
Drag callbacks supply local and world matrices and related data. This demo decomposes the local matrix into position, rotation and scale for display; coordinate spaces must match business data.
purposeDetails: An editor often needs to rotate or scale around an edge even when the object origin is elsewhere. PivotControls combines an adjustable pivot, gizmos and matrix callbacks.
It does not implement business undo, persistence or physics constraints. Compare TransformControls for conventional axis transforms and DragControls for simple planar dragging.
codeDetails: The component wraps the model; offset or anchor positions the pivot, and onDrag supplies matrices from handle interaction.

The example decomposes the callback’s local matrix for position, Euler rotation and scale. Compare rotation paths after changing the pivot, keeping in mind local values and world positions need not match.

conceptDetails: Resize calculates a uniform scale from child bounds to normalize a selected dimension. By default it makes the longest side one scene unit while preserving proportions.
For bounds 4 × 2 × 1 m, the default scale factor is 1/4, producing approximately 1 × 0.5 × 0.25 m. It scales the wrapped group rather than editing the original model file.
A specific width, height or depth can be selected as the basis. Other axes use the same factor, so the longest side need not then equal one.
purposeDetails: Assets of inconsistent sizes often need bounds measurement and a calculated factor for thumbnails or previews. Resize packages that process.
Normalization changes actual scene scale and is unsuitable as-is for engineering measurement or physics that must preserve real dimensions. Center adjusts position and does not replace resizing.
codeDetails: Wrap the object in Resize; the default uses its longest side and width, height or depth can select a basis axis. The result is uniformly scaled.
The demo compares original and processed models, changing width and height to observe the longest side; disable processing to compare the original dimensions.

conceptDetails: BBAnchor positions children from a parent object’s bounding box. The box is an axis-aligned extent enclosing the object; the demo uses an orange sphere to show the computed anchor.

conceptDetails: Bounds measures target object bounds and provides camera framing. A bounding box summarizes the target’s spatial extent; framing uses that extent, viewport and margin to fit it into the view.
When one viewer loads different-sized models, a fixed camera distance can crop a large model or make a small one tiny. Measuring the current target before fitting adapts framing to its dimensions.
After geometry dimensions change, earlier measurements can be stale. In this demo the fit button refreshes the bounds before fitting again.
purposeDetails: Manual framing requires calculating object extents, camera projection, viewport ratio and target distance. Bounds combines these steps and can cooperate with camera controls.
A bounding box approximates extent and is not necessarily the object contour or the best artistic composition; occlusion, complex hierarchies and controller state still need scene-specific handling.
codeDetails: Wrap targets in Bounds and use its API to refresh and fit; margin adds room around the target.

conceptDetails: useBounds obtains an imperative interface from the nearest Bounds context so descendants can refresh object bounds and adjust camera framing or clipping. It does not create the Bounds container and cannot be used outside it.

conceptDetails: A plane normally retains its own rotation and can appear edge-on when the camera moves sideways. Billboard adjusts its inner group to align with camera orientation while keeping its 3D scene position.

Consider DOM for web buttons, forms or selectable text. A label that must occupy a real world position should not use ScreenSpace merely because it faces the camera.

conceptDetails: With a perspective camera, equal world-sized objects usually appear smaller as they move farther away. ScreenSizer adjusts group scale using camera, object position and canvas size to keep an object near a desired screen-pixel size.
It changes the object’s world scale rather than camera projection. World dimensions vary with camera distance, so the result should not simultaneously be treated as a physical-size measurement.
The indigo demo plane uses screen-size scaling; the amber plane keeps fixed world dimensions. Move the camera to distinguish stable screen size from fixed world size.
purposeDetails: Hotspots at different depths can become hard to see or click when they retain identical world dimensions. ScreenSizer converts a pixel target to a corresponding scale for visual usability.

Automatic scaling can mislead when product dimensions or physical collision must remain true to scale; manage visual markers and real objects separately. The result also depends on camera and viewport.

conceptDetails: calculateScaleFactor is a calculation function: from a world position, camera, viewport and target pixel distance, it estimates the corresponding world-space length. It returns a number and does not create or scale an object.

Under perspective projection, one meter occupies different pixel widths near and far from the camera. Keeping a unit-width plane at the same pixel width across depths requires recalculating its world size at its position.
The amber demo plane remains one meter wide; the indigo plane uses the calculated width. Their screen appearance differs as camera distance changes.
purposeDetails: A returned value is useful when application code must combine position, pixel target and custom scaling logic. ScreenSizer is suitable when a component should manage scaling automatically.

The calculation depends on the actual camera, viewport and target position. Parent transforms, original child geometry and occlusion can also affect apparent size; the returned number is not a direct pixel width for every object.
codeDetails: The function projects a world position, offsets it by the requested pixels on screen, unprojects and measures a world distance; the caller chooses how to use the number.
The example applies the result to a unit plane, then varies camera distance and pixel target. A non-unit base geometry also needs its original dimensions considered.

Environmental reflection and visible background are separate settings: a map can affect materials while the background stays unchanged; enabling background also displays the environment behind the scene.

purposeDetails: Product viewers often need controlled surrounding reflections. Loading and assigning a map separately for every material duplicates work; Environment combines common sources with scene-level settings.

conceptDetails: EnvironmentMap accepts an existing Texture and applies it to the scene environment, optionally as background. It handles scene assignment rather than choosing how files are loaded.
For example, an environment texture obtained elsewhere can be passed to EnvironmentMap. Scene materials receive reflection from environment, while background decides whether it is directly visible.
Texture source and lifetime remain the responsibility of its creator or loader; assigning a scene texture does not create physical background geometry.
purposeDetails: An application may already have an environment map from a hook, cache or custom pipeline. EnvironmentMap reuses that result without repeating loading configuration at the scene assignment point.
For only one material, assigning envMap directly may suffice. Shared textures need clear ownership so resources still in use are not disposed early.
codeDetails: The demo first loads six faces with useEnvironment, then passes the result to <EnvironmentMap map={texture} /> and controls the background separately.

conceptDetails: EnvironmentPortal captures a separate child scene with a cube camera and applies the resulting environment texture to the main scene. Bright shapes or backgrounds in that child scene become reflected regions on materials.

For example, a white rectangle in the virtual environment can create a bright stripe on a metal sphere; moving it requires a fresh capture. Child-scene objects are not automatically physical objects in the main scene.
resolution controls captured texture size and frames controls update count. This demo uses frames={1} for a static capture; dynamic environments need an update-frequency and cost decision.
purposeDetails: When no suitable HDR environment exists or reflection shapes need art direction, a virtual capture-only scene can be constructed. EnvironmentPortal manages capture and scene environment application.
Six-direction capture costs rendering work, and the resulting map is still an environment approximation rather than automatic local occlusion or all direct lighting.
codeDetails: Place an environment background and meshes under EnvironmentPortal and set resolution, frames and background.
The demo captures a background color and white plane, then the metal sphere samples the result. Background visibility and environment intensity show different aspects of scene assignment.

conceptDetails: useEnvironment loads and returns an environment texture from files or a preset. It supplies texture data; it does not itself assign scene.environment or automatically display a background.
The caller can assign the returned texture to one material’s envMap or pass it to EnvironmentMap for scene assignment. Material-level maps and scene-level environment have different scopes.

purposeDetails: Returning a texture is flexible when an application manages scenes itself or wants only specific objects to reflect an environment. The hook packages loading logic for supported resources.
Environment may be more direct for declarative scene-wide setup. Remote assets, format support and shared texture lifetime remain application concerns.

parameters: Material ref and shader compilation callback.

conceptDetails: An ordinary environment map is often treated as infinitely distant: changing reflection direction reveals different content, but translating an object in a room may not produce plausible parallax for nearby walls. useBoxProjectedEnv corrects sampling direction using a box position and size as an approximation of finite space.

Imagine the environment projected onto room bounds: the reflected ray’s relationship with the box affects sampling direction. Changing box width or object position can shift bright regions relative to ordinary infinite-environment sampling.
This is still a box approximation; it does not build actual room geometry or trace all dynamic occlusion. A box that does not match the environment can look unnatural.
purposeDetails: Indoor displays and nearby rooms need reflections that respond to object position. Box projection provides an approximation more appropriate than infinite-distance sampling without capturing an environment for every object.
Non-box spaces, dynamic occlusion and complex reflections may not suit this approximation; material and Three.js shader injection compatibility also need validation.
codeDetails: Call useBoxProjectedEnv(center, size) to obtain material configuration and use it with an environment map on a compatible material.

This project uses Three.js r186; the example calls the hook’s onBeforeCompile and adapts current shader injection points. Both sides use the same environment so ordinary and corrected reflections can be compared.

parameters: Minimum movement before a sample is added.

conceptDetails: Trail continually samples a moving target and uses MeshLine to render a ribbon from recent positions. It follows the first 3D child by default or an explicit target.
Successive recorded positions form a path; as old samples are replaced by new ones, earlier parts leave the visible trail. It shows recent motion rather than predicting the future route.
width controls ribbon width, while length and sampling settings affect retained history. Apparent length also depends on target speed and sampling.
purposeDetails: A flying object, pointer or moving marker may need a motion cue. Trail combines position sampling and rendering instead of requiring a custom buffer and line material.
It suits visual trails; useTrail is preferable when drawing custom particles, analyzing sampled data or owning line geometry.
codeDetails: Place the target inside Trail or specify target, then set width, length, color and attenuation; the component renders a ribbon from its samples.

conceptDetails: useTrail samples a target position and returns a ref containing a Float32Array. The array stores trail coordinates, but the hook creates no mesh, line or material.

Sampling can use local or world positions; choose a coordinate space consistent with the subsequent rendering object. Target movement, sample interval and length together determine retained positions.
Because data lives in a ref and updates per frame, consumers generally read or copy it in the frame loop rather than assuming each update triggers a React render.
purposeDetails: Direct samples offer flexibility for custom lines, particles or other effects. For a standard visible ribbon, the Trail component is more direct.
The caller owns buffer updates, coordinate space and cleanup. Samples are not a complete rendered effect on their own.

parameters: Returns true when every alpha is zero.
conceptDetails: A sprite frame can be fully transparent or contain visible pixels. checkIfFrameIsEmpty scans alpha channels in an RGBA array: any nonzero alpha returns false; all zero returns true.
For [255, 255, 255, 0], RGB is white but alpha is zero, so the pixel is considered empty. Changing alpha to 1 or 255 makes it nonempty. The test uses transparency, not whether color is black.
The function only inspects supplied pixels; it does not load a sheet, split frames or play animation. An empty array also returns true because no nonzero alpha is found.
purposeDetails: Grid-based sprite sheets may contain blank cells. Detecting completely transparent cells can help a loader mark empty frames rather than treat them as image content.
It does not decide whether a frame is nearly transparent, visually similar or meaningful. Even one very small nonzero alpha makes it nonempty.
codeDetails: Prepare an RGBA pixel array, call checkIfFrameIsEmpty(pixels) and read the boolean.

conceptDetails: A sprite sheet places multiple frames in one texture. useSpriteLoader loads the texture and optional frame metadata, organizing a spriteObj suitable for SpriteAnimator.

This example passes no JSON and specifies four frames, so the loader infers an equal-sized grid from image dimensions and frame count; it also reads pixels to detect empty transparent cells. If the source layout does not match that inference, supply suitable frame data or another parser.
Loading and playback are separate: the hook prepares texture and frames, while SpriteAnimator changes the current frame. The caller handles the state before spriteObj exists.
purposeDetails: Preparing texture, frame coordinates and empty-frame information repeatedly is cumbersome. useSpriteLoader combines resource preparation so an animator can use the result.
Pixel reading can be restricted by cross-origin rules; validate compatibility and failure handling for uneven grids, packed formats and dynamic resources.

conceptDetails: ContactShadows captures scene depth from the receiver plane’s direction, blurs the result and projects it onto the plane as a soft contact shadow. It is not the main light’s ordinary shadow map.

purposeDetails: It is suited to a particular receiver plane, not an accurate light shadow on arbitrary surfaces. Live updates and blur cost resources; static content can consider limiting update frames.

conceptDetails: AccumulativeShadows accumulates multiple lighting and shadow samples into a planar light map. Each sample differs slightly; blending them produces a softer result that stabilizes over time.
In temporal mode the work spans multiple frames: count increases from zero to frames and accumulation stops at the target. The first visible shadow is not necessarily the final stable result.

purposeDetails: Sampling requires time and resources, and frequently moving scenes may repeatedly reset. Compare ContactShadows for a simpler live contact-shadow approach.

conceptDetails: accumulativeContext is the React context supplied by AccumulativeShadows, exposing reset, update, getMesh, count and light registration. It is not an independent shadow-rendering component.
A descendant can inspect accumulation count or call reset when scene conditions change. Count describes the sampling process, not a direct shadow-quality or performance score.
In the demo count grows again toward the target after an object moves or accumulation restarts. This is real container state, and the context must be used under its provider.
purposeDetails: It does not decide every reset condition for the application. Repeated resets in a continuously changing scene can prevent shadows from stabilizing.
codeDetails: Use useContext(accumulativeContext) inside an AccumulativeShadows child; reset restarts accumulation and count can be observed as progress.
The example Observer accesses the context to reset; the demo reports real count while AccumulativeShadows sets target frames.

conceptDetails: SpotLightShadow is a child of Drei SpotLight that uses a texture or shader mask in the light path to project a pattern. It depends on its parent spotlight and is not an independent light.

The example shader creates stripes: different mask regions occlude the light path differently, producing stripes on the floor. Moving the mask or light changes projection; the pattern is not a texture painted onto the floor material.
Mask distance and size interact with spotlight angle to determine the projected area; shadow settings and a receiver are also required.
purposeDetails: This is a real-time shadow projection rather than complete simulation of light through complex media; fine stripes and distant projections can be limited by shadow-map resolution.
codeDetails: Add SpotLightShadow inside SpotLight, supply a shader or texture mask and set projection parameters such as distance and scale.

conceptDetails: Caustics are bright patterns formed when refracted or reflected light concentrates in areas. Caustics estimates refraction from information such as depth and normals, then projects the result onto a receiver plane as a real-time approximation.
Sphere shape, refractive index, light direction and height above the ground all affect the pattern. Intensity changes brightness rather than guaranteeing physical energy conservation.
The demo receiver faces +Y. Changing height and light direction changes projected position and shape; this is not a universal caustics simulation for every surface orientation.
purposeDetails: Ordinary real-time transmission or refraction materials do not automatically produce focused-light patterns on the ground. Caustics provides a configurable approximation for glass or crystal displays.
The result depends on sampling and scene assumptions and may require quality/performance tuning. Physically precise optics or arbitrary complex receivers need other approaches.
codeDetails: Place the caustic-producing object under Caustics and configure refractive index, light direction, intensity and receiver settings.

conceptDetails: Edges extracts line segments from its parent mesh geometry. It compares adjacent face angles and draws edges exceeding threshold; boundary edges can also be retained. The output is attached lines, not a modification to the parent geometry.

Think of a cube edge as the meeting of two faces: the edge is drawn when the angle meets the threshold condition. Raising the threshold generally retains fewer edges; line width changes appearance, not selection.

This differs from drawing every triangle edge in a wireframe: coplanar triangle diagonals are typically excluded by the angle threshold. Geometry, face relationships and threshold all affect the result.
purposeDetails: Compare Wireframe for full triangle topology and Outlines for the outer silhouette rather than internal geometric edges.
codeDetails: Place Edges inside the target mesh so it reads parent geometry; threshold filters angles, while lineWidth and color control appearance.
The demo adjusts threshold and width and can disable the effect for comparison. Lines follow parent transforms without modifying its geometry or creating solid borders.

conceptDetails: MeshDistortMaterial offsets vertices with time-varying noise in the vertex shader, creating an undulating mesh while retaining the base physical material’s appearance capabilities.
The deformation happens during rendering. A mesh needs enough vertices to show smooth changes: a low-subdivision sphere can look coarse even with a larger amplitude.

conceptDetails: MeshWobbleMaterial rotates vertices and normals in the vertex shader based on height and time, producing periodic twisting. It extends a standard material rather than rebuilding geometry on the CPU.
Vertices at different heights receive different rotations, so a sufficiently subdivided box can visibly twist. With too few vertices the shape cannot bend smoothly.
factor controls wobble amount and speed controls animation rate. Increasing speed makes motion faster without directly increasing amplitude.
purposeDetails: Rendered deformation is not a physics constraint: actual geometry data, collision and picking may not follow it. Precise interaction may require another approach.
codeDetails: Apply MeshWobbleMaterial to a sufficiently subdivided mesh and set factor and speed; standard material properties still control its surface.

conceptDetails: GradientTexture draws a gradient into a Canvas from color stops and creates a CanvasTexture that a material can sample, usually attaching to map as a material child.

A linear gradient transitions along a direction; a radial gradient transitions outward from a center. stops and colors pair positions with colors; moving a middle stop changes the transition, not the mesh position.
Texture resolution affects sampling detail and plane UVs determine how the gradient maps onto the surface. Generating a texture does not create scene geometry.
purposeDetails: Color stops can generate procedural gradients without preparing a separate image for every color combination.
It suits relatively simple gradients; complex real-time gradients or custom blending may be better served by a shader.

conceptDetails: useVideoTexture creates and returns a Three.js VideoTexture after waiting for video metadata. Its image source is a video element rather than a static picture.

Video frame changes update the texture during playback; pausing can leave the current frame visible. texture.image exposes the underlying video element, but playback requests remain subject to browser policy.
This demo sets start false, mutes and loops the local video and starts it from user action. Video dimensions and plane dimensions differ; plane width and height determine the scene display area.
purposeDetails: The hook provides direct access to the texture and video element when React components need playback state or custom material composition.
Applications must handle encoding support, autoplay restrictions, cross-origin rules and media cleanup; the hook cannot guarantee arbitrary video playback in every browser.
codeDetails: Call useVideoTexture(src, options), assign texture to material map and request texture.image.play() from a user action.
The demo uses a local muted video; play and pause affect the underlying video without removing the plane.

conceptDetails: MeshDiscardMaterial discards surface fragments, so that material does not draw a visible surface. The mesh and geometry still exist; children and other rendering passes need not disappear.

The demo discards the cube surface while attached edges remain visible and the shadow pass still produces a shadow. Visibility, event picking and shadows are separate mechanisms, so a hidden surface does not establish the behavior of the others.
discard is a fragment-shader operation, not deletion, geometry disposal or removal from the scene.
purposeDetails: Some effects hide a solid surface while keeping edges or a shadow, such as an outline-only marker. This material provides a way to handle the visible surface.
Do not use it as a permissions or data-hiding mechanism. If the object should not participate in rendering and interaction, remove or disable it as appropriate.

conceptDetails: MultiMaterial applies child materials to the same parent mesh and creates a full-geometry group for each material. The renderer can therefore draw the same geometry once per material.
For example, the first layer uses a solid material and the second uses wireframe. Both share geometry but determine their own color and rendering; changing wireframe opacity affects only that layer.
Shared geometry does not imply one draw. Material count, transparent-layer sorting and depth settings affect performance and the final overlay.
purposeDetails: Layering solid and wireframe effects on one object can otherwise require duplicated mesh and transform management. MultiMaterial combines materials on the same geometry.
It is not the only way to assign materials to different regions; many layers add drawing work and require validation of transparency order and depth conflicts.
codeDetails: Place MultiMaterial inside the parent mesh and provide child materials in order; it creates a full-geometry group for each.
The example uses a standard solid layer and a transparent wireframe layer, whose opacity is adjusted by the slider. Geometry is shared, but each material requires its own draw.

conceptDetails: Wireframe uses triangle barycentric coordinates and a shader to draw edges with configurable width, dashes and fill. It shows rendered triangle topology, not just the outer silhouette.
A face that looks quadrilateral is commonly made from two triangles, so wireframe may show a diagonal. That is triangulation, not necessarily a damaged model.
The line effect is a render layer and does not create physical line-tube geometry. Thickness, repeats and fill affect appearance.
purposeDetails: Teaching, debugging and stylized displays can benefit from mesh topology with adjustable line width or dashes. Wireframe supplies shader-based edge rendering.
Compare Edges for significant face-angle edges and Outlines for the outer silhouette. Validate compatibility and cost for complex or dynamically deformed geometry.
codeDetails: Place Wireframe inside the parent mesh; stroke sets color, thickness sets width, and dash with dashRepeats controls dashes.

conceptDetails: MeshReflectorMaterial renders the scene from a virtual camera into a texture and samples it in a plane material to create dynamic reflection. The reflection comes from an additional scene render, not automatic inference of all objects from a static environment map.
Plane orientation, camera and scene content determine what appears in the texture. Reflection strength changes the blend with the base surface; blur spreads detail to suggest a rougher appearance.
Render-target resolution and blur affect both clarity and cost. It is primarily for planar reflection, not a general curved-surface or full ray-tracing solution.
purposeDetails: Floors, mirror walls and display counters may need to reflect moving scene objects that a static environment map cannot update automatically. The material combines capture and blending.
Reflection needs additional rendering; multiple reflectors or high resolution add cost. Validate transparent objects, occlusion and edges in the actual scene.
codeDetails: Attach the material to the reflective plane and configure resolution, blending and blur; captured scene objects provide reflection content.
The demo changes reflection strength and blur while rotating the view. Compare reflected detail with the base floor color to distinguish material blending from real object position.

conceptDetails: Transmission samples and distorts the scene behind an object to create a glass-like appearance. MeshTransmissionMaterial builds on a physical material with a scene buffer and controls such as roughness and dispersion.
Imagine stripes behind a sphere: index of refraction and thickness alter sampling direction and offset so the stripes appear bent; higher roughness blurs transmitted detail.

The effect depends on what is captured in its buffer. Render order, other transparent objects and sampling settings can change the result; it is a real-time approximation, not a complete physical light path.
purposeDetails: Glass products and transparent decoration need the background to remain visible while showing refraction and surface character. This material packages the sampling and visual controls.
Scene buffering and multiple samples add cost. Validate overlapping transparent objects, dynamic backgrounds and mobile devices in the actual scene.
codeDetails: Use MeshTransmissionMaterial on a mesh; transmission controls transmission, while ior, thickness and roughness affect refraction, path approximation and blur.
The demo keeps background stripes fixed and varies index of refraction, thickness and roughness. samples and resolution affect sampling quality and cost, not mesh subdivisions.

parameters: Approximate dispersion with fewer ray samples.
conceptDetails: MeshRefractionMaterial uses a BVH built from the target geometry to accelerate internal ray calculations, then samples an environment map along refracted directions for a gem-like effect.

Index of refraction affects how directions change entering or leaving a medium; bounce count affects internal tracing work, and dispersion offsets color channels. Together they change how the environment appears in the crystal.
Both sides of the demo use the same six-face environment map; the right can switch to refraction. The result depends on environment and geometry, not full physical ray tracing of the dynamic scene.
purposeDetails: Crystals and gems need complex-looking changes to their environment through refraction. This material packages BVH construction, ray direction calculations and environment sampling.
Dynamic deformation, non-closed or complex geometry and high bounce counts can introduce limitations and cost. Validate on target devices and do not treat the image as precise optical measurement.
codeDetails: Attach MeshRefractionMaterial to the target mesh and provide an environment map, index of refraction and tracing parameters; it builds an acceleration structure from geometry.
The example compares ordinary and refractive materials with the same environment, then adjusts parameters. The environment supplies sampled content and the material determines its presentation.

conceptDetails: shaderMaterial is a factory: it accepts uniform defaults plus GLSL vertex and fragment shaders and returns a ShaderMaterial subclass. It is not itself a React component that draws the screen.
A uniform is an updateable input to a shader. Here split controls the color transition: the slider changes split and the fragment shader recalculates color from UV without replacing geometry.
The factory creates property accessors for uniforms. Once registered with R3F extend, they can be set as JSX props; projection, color and other shader behavior still need to be authored.
purposeDetails: Custom effects often need React state passed to GLSL. Directly managing nested uniforms.value can be cumbersome; shaderMaterial generates a material class with declarative access.
It does not guarantee shader correctness, cross-device compatibility or physical lighting. GLSL inputs, render state and performance remain the author’s responsibility.
codeDetails: The factory creates a class from { split: 0.5 } and two GLSL sources; extend registers it for <lessonGradientMaterial split={...} />.
The vertex shader passes UV and calculates projected position; the fragment shader reads split and blends two colors. The slider updates a uniform, not plane vertices.

conceptDetails: A transparent visible material changes the surface appearance, but the depth pass used by shadow maps may not represent transparency the same way. ShadowAlpha supplies custom depth and distance materials for its parent mesh and approximates transparent shadows with dithering.

Dithering retains and discards some shadow samples to suggest light transmission; it does not trace continuous physical light through the object. Shadow-map resolution, sampling and lights affect the result.
The demo uses equal surface opacity on two objects but ShadowAlpha only on the right. Their ground shadows distinguish surface transparency from shadow treatment.
purposeDetails: Transparent panels or thin decorations may need a lighter ground shadow than the default opaque-looking shadow. ShadowAlpha offers an approximate shadow-rendering approach.
It does not model accurate colored transmission or complex medium absorption. Choose an appropriate renderer for physically precise results and inspect dithering at target resolution.
codeDetails: Place ShadowAlpha inside a castShadow mesh and set opacity; the light must cast shadows and the ground must receive them.
The example compares an ordinary transparent object with one using ShadowAlpha. Visible material opacity and shadow-material opacity are configured separately and should be coordinated.

conceptDetails: RenderTexture renders a child scene into an offscreen texture and can attach it directly to a parent material property. The plane in the main scene is one object; the rotating model shown on it belongs to another render scene.

purposeDetails: Displaying an independent scene on a mesh otherwise requires managing a render target, portal, camera and render order. RenderTexture packages that workflow.
The child scene adds rendering work; complexity and resolution increase cost. It does not automatically isolate every interaction or guarantee unlimited recursion.

conceptDetails: Mask writes an id into the stencil buffer using geometry. The stencil buffer stores render-time region markers; Mask normally does not write visible color or depth.

For example, a circular Mask writes id=1 and materials using the matching stencil test draw stripes only where the test passes. Circle position and radius define the marked region without changing stripe geometry.
Canvas must enable stencil and writing must occur before reading. Inversion comes from the receiving material’s test rather than cutting geometry out of the scene.
purposeDetails: Circular windows, local displays and area masking need to constrain where materials draw. Mask provides declarative stencil writing without manually configuring every stencil state.
Stencil masking is a rendering rule, not geometry modification or a security boundary. IDs, draw order and buffer settings affect results.
codeDetails: Enable stencil, create <Mask id={1}> with circle geometry and apply useMask(1) settings to receiving materials.
The demo moves and resizes the circle. Inverse mode retains the same written id but changes the receiving test.

conceptDetails: useMask returns material stencil properties for an id and inverse option. It neither writes the mask nor creates geometry; a Mask or equivalent must first write the corresponding value.
For example, if Mask writes id=1 inside a circle, useMask(1) makes a material draw in matching regions; useMask(1, true) uses an inverse test to draw outside them.

purposeDetails: When several materials should obey one mask, manually matching stencilFunc, ref and related properties can be error-prone. useMask returns configuration for the selected id.
It depends on an enabled stencil buffer and correct draw order. A visual mask does not change collision, geometry or data access.
codeDetails: Call useMask(1, inverse) and spread the result onto each receiving material; the corresponding Mask writes id=1.

parameters: True for objects except arrays and functions; otherwise false.
conceptDetails: IsObject is a predicate used by the texture loader: the current implementation checks value === Object(value) and excludes arrays and functions to distinguish object input from other forms.
For example { map: path } returns true, while a path string and an array return false. Date is also an object, so the result does not mean “plain dictionary” or “valid texture configuration.”
Although JavaScript reports typeof null as object, this function returns false for null because null is not equal to Object(null). It is not a complete input validator.
purposeDetails: A texture loader must distinguish a single path, an array and a named object to produce corresponding result shapes. This predicate supports that type branch.
It does not validate URL availability, object fields or plain-object structure. Business input still needs dedicated validation.
codeDetails: Call IsObject(value) and read the boolean; the example compares an object, array and string.
The demo also includes null, number, date and function inputs. Results come directly from the installed version to expose the predicate’s boundaries.

conceptDetails: Progress provides shared loading state through a function child, including active, progress, loaded, total and errors. The caller decides how to present those values.

The demo issues local requests and adds a short wait after success for observation; panel state reflects the registered demonstration process.
